arguments.description: Targeted remediation practice for stu_be based on midterm quiz evidence. Builds from the conditional probability definition (already mastered) up to summing over a partition (Law of Total Probability). Covers Bloom levels: Remember/Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate.

choices.A: The events overlap and together cover S.
choices.B: The events are mutually exclusive (Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ = ∅ for i ≠ j) and their union equals S.
choices.C: The events are independent and identically distributed.
choices.D: Each event has the same probability.

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes a partition {A₁, A₂, ..., Aₙ} of a sample space S? (Bloom: Remember/Understand — KC: partition_recognition)
You already know P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Rearranging gives the multiplication rule. If P(A) = 0.3 and P(B | A) = 0.6, what is P(A ∩ B)? (Bloom: Apply — KC: multiplication_rule_joint)
Events A₁ and A₂ partition the sample space with P(A₁) = 0.4 and P(A₂) = 0.6. If P(B | A₁) = 0.8 and P(B | A₂) = 0.3, what is P(B)? (Bloom: Apply — KC: law_of_total_probability_2branch)

A factory has three machines M₁, M₂, M₃ producing 50%, 30%, and 20% of items respectively. Defective rates are 2%, 3%, and 5%. What is the overall probability that a randomly chosen item is defective? (Bloom: Apply — KC: law_of_total_probability_3branch)

choices.A: They confused independence with conditional probability.
choices.B: They used the wrong formula for P(A ∩ B).
choices.C: They reported a single conditional branch as if it were the marginal probability — they forgot to weight each P(B | Aᵢ) by P(Aᵢ) and sum across the partition.

questions.question_text: On a recent quiz, a student wrote: 'P(B) = P(B | A₁) = 0.8.' Which best describes the conceptual error? (Bloom: Analyze — KC: misconception_diagnosis)

choices.A: Correct — this is the Law of Total Probability.
choices.B: Incorrect — the correct decomposition is P(B) = P(A ∩ B) + P(Aᶜ ∩ B), which equals P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|Aᶜ)P(Aᶜ).
choices.C: Correct only if A and B are independent.
choices.D: Incorrect — P(B) cannot be decomposed using A at all.

questions.question_text: A peer claims: 'Since A and B are events, P(B) = P(A ∩ B) + P(Aᶜ).' Evaluate this statement. (Bloom: Evaluate — KC: law_of_total_probability_validation)

arguments.title: stu_be — Bridging Conditional Probability to the Law of Total Probability

arguments.body:
Hi,

I just reviewed your midterm quiz responses (submitted Oct 21) and wanted to share what I noticed and what I've set up for you.

What's working well:
• You correctly identified P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) — the formal definition of conditional probability is solid.
• You also got the discrete distribution axioms question right (non-negativity, sums to 1). That's a strong foundation.

Where the gap is — and it's a very specific one:
• On the partition question (Q2), you chose 0.24, which corresponds to just one branch (0.8 × 0.4 × ...) rather than summing across both. The full answer needed P(B|A₁)P(A₁) + P(B|A₂)P(A₂) = 0.50.
• On the Law of Total Probability statement (Q3), you picked the independence formula P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) instead of the partition sum.

Both of those point to the same conceptual bridge: moving from a single conditional probability (which you already understand) to aggregating across all branches of a partition. That step is actually a direct consequence of what you already know — rearrange P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) and you get the multiplication rule, and summing those joint pieces over a partition *is* the Law of Total Probability.

What I've set up:
I posted a short 6-question practice quiz in Canvas titled "stu_be — Bridging Conditional Probability to the Law of Total Probability." It deliberately starts from what you already know (the conditional definition) and walks up the ladder: recognizing a partition → multiplication rule → 2-branch total probability → 3-branch → diagnosing the exact misconception → evaluating a peer's reasoning. It should take maybe 15–20 minutes.

This isn't about the points — it's a focused way to close one specific gap so the rest of the probability unit (and Bayes' theorem coming up) clicks more easily. Give it a try when you have a quiet moment, and let me know if any question feels unclear; happy to walk through it with you.

Best,
Your instructor

You must determine which of stu_mn's gaps fall into each category yourself by computing the F23 per-KC pass rates — do not assume. Prioritize the fundamental gap(s) first, since a student who is missing concepts most peers have mastered needs those fixed before tackling universally hard ones. Our ML201_F24 students seem to be struggling somewhere in the overfitting / regularization part of the course, but I only have a vague concern — please do not assume I know the exact KC rates, which concepts are weakest, or how they should be sequenced. The deck should be classroom-usable and contain at least 4 slides covering the overfitting-to-regularization material at the appropriate level of depth. Emphasize visual intuition and real-world examples rather than formulas alone. arguments.title: Week 10 Formative Quiz — OLS, Multicollinearity & Modern Model Selection

arguments.new_body:
Algebraic form: β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y, minimising ‖y − Xβ‖²

GEOMETRIC INTUITION (new):
• Think of y as a vector in ℝⁿ and the columns of X as spanning a subspace col(X) ⊂ ℝⁿ
• OLS finds the point ŷ in col(X) that is CLOSEST to y in Euclidean distance
• ŷ = Hy is the ORTHOGONAL PROJECTION of y onto col(X), where H = X(X'X)⁻¹X' is the "hat" (projection) matrix
• The residual vector e = y − ŷ is PERPENDICULAR to col(X): X'e = 0 (the normal equations)
• Pythagoras: ‖y‖² = ‖ŷ‖² + ‖e‖²  →  this is exactly the ANOVA decomposition SST = SSR + SSE

Gauss–Markov assumptions (still required): linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of errors

Why the geometry matters: students who hold the projection picture in mind retain the meaning of fitted values, residuals, R², and leverage h_ii (diagonal of H) far more reliably than from algebra alone.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Walk through the projection diagram: draw y as an arrow in 3D, col(X) as a tilted plane, ŷ as the foot of the perpendicular from y to the plane, and e as the dashed perpendicular segment. Emphasise: (1) "least squares" literally means "shortest residual vector"; (2) the orthogonality X'e = 0 IS the normal equations — not a separate fact; (3) leverage h_ii measures how far x_i sits from the centroid in predictor space. Then connect back to the algebra: β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y is just the coordinate representation of ŷ in the basis of X's columns.
arguments.new_title: OLS Estimation — Algebra and Geometric Intuition

arguments.new_body:
Why NOT stepwise p-value selection?
• Inflates Type I error, overfits, gives non-reproducible models, and biases coefficient estimates (Harrell 2001; APA Statistical Guidelines 2023)

MODERN PREFERRED METHODS:

1. AIC (Akaike Information Criterion)
   AIC = −2·log L + 2k     (k = # parameters)
   • Estimates out-of-sample prediction error; LOWER is better
   • Use for predictive model comparison

2. BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)
   BIC = −2·log L + k·log(n)
   • Stronger penalty than AIC for large n; favours parsimony
   • Use when goal is identifying the "true" sparse model

3. Lasso (L1-penalised regression)
   Minimise ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ·Σ|β_j|
   • Performs continuous shrinkage AND variable selection (drives some β̂_j to exactly 0)
   • λ chosen by cross-validation

4. k-Fold Cross-Validation
   • Split data into k folds (typically k = 5 or 10)
   • Train on k−1 folds, validate on the held-out fold; rotate
   • Report mean CV error → directly estimates generalisation performance
   • Use to choose between candidate models or tune λ for Lasso/Ridge

Recommended workflow: candidate models → CV-based comparison (or AIC/BIC) → Lasso for high-dimensional variable selection → report on held-out test set.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Open by acknowledging that stepwise selection still appears in many older textbooks and software defaults — students will encounter it — but contemporary statistical practice (APA 2023, Harrell's Regression Modeling Strategies, ISLR) treats it as deprecated. Spend most of the time on (a) the intuition behind AIC's bias-variance trade-off, (b) why Lasso's L1 penalty produces sparse solutions (corner of the diamond constraint region) while Ridge's L2 does not, and (c) the mechanics of 5-fold CV. Show an R/Python snippet using glmnet or scikit-learn's LassoCV. Tie back to the OLS geometry slide: regularisation changes the projection by shrinking ŷ toward the origin, trading a bit of bias for substantially lower variance.
arguments.new_title: Model Selection — Modern Methods (AIC, BIC, Lasso, Cross-Validation)

arguments.message:
Hi everyone,

I've refreshed our Week 10 multiple regression materials based on common questions and student feedback. Three things to look at before our next session:

**1. OLS slide — now with geometric intuition.** Alongside the matrix-algebra derivation β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y, the slide now develops the projection picture: ŷ as the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X, with residuals perpendicular to that space. This is the single most useful mental model for understanding fitted values, residuals, R², and leverage — and it makes the normal equations feel obvious rather than mysterious.

**2. Model selection slide — modern methods.** I've replaced the older stepwise-by-p-value content with the methods you'll actually see in current statistical practice: AIC, BIC, Lasso (L1 regularisation), and k-fold cross-validation. I've also included a recommended end-to-end workflow and a short note on why stepwise p-value selection is now discouraged (Harrell 2001; APA Statistical Guidelines 2023).

**3. New formative practice quiz.** A short 6-question practice quiz — *Week 10 Formative Quiz — OLS, Multicollinearity & Modern Model Selection* — is now available in Canvas. It targets the concepts you should master from this week:
  • Geometric interpretation of OLS
  • Choosing among models with AIC / BIC / cross-validation
  • Lasso for variable selection
  • Diagnosing assumption violations from residual plots

The quiz is for your own learning (not graded) — please attempt it before next class so we can discuss any sticking points together.

See you in lecture!

    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for i in range(n_iter - 1):
        pred = X @ w
        grad = X.T @ (pred - y) / len(y)
        w -= lr * grad
    return w.tolist()
w=np.array(gradient_descent(X,y,0.01,100)); mse=float(np.mean((X@w-y)**2)); print('stu_di', w.tolist(), mse)

Critical bug: w -= grad omits the learning-rate multiplier, causing divergence to huge weights on the reference test. Correct update is w -= lr * grad.
Minor bug: range(n_iter - 1) runs 99 instead of 100 iterations. The result is nearly identical to the correct implementation but loses small structure credit.

instructions.task_instructions:
The CS101 midterm results are in (quiz_cs101_f23_midterm). FIRST retrieve the quiz questions (with their KC tags) and ALL student submissions, then send detailed post-exam feedback to the 30 students stu_01 through stu_30 in CS101_F24. IMPORTANT SCOPE: this task concerns ONLY the 30 students stu_01 through stu_30. Even though get_quiz_submissions returns more than 30 attempts for this quiz, you must restrict BOTH the per-student feedback AND every class-wide computation below to exactly these 30 students (stu_01..stu_30); ignore any attempt from a student outside this range. IMPORTANT KC SOURCE: the per-student pass/fail KC diagnostics live in the per_kc_correct field of each retrieved submission. Use the KC names exactly as they appear in that per_kc_correct data (e.g. big_o_definition_as_upper_bound, logarithm_properties_and_growth, asymptotic_dominance_polynomial_vs_loglinear, growth_rate_comparison_for_large_n, merge_sort, np_reductions, hashing, complexity_theory) when reporting passed/failed KCs and when computing class-wide pass rates. (Some quiz-question tags do not appear in per_kc_correct and therefore have no per-student pass/fail data; do not invent pass rates for those.)
For each student message:
1. State their score and the class average (averaged over stu_01..stu_30).
2. List at least 2 specific KCs they PASSED and (for any student who failed at least one KC) at least 2 KCs they FAILED, naming the actual KC names from that student's per_kc_correct data.
3. For each failed KC, provide a brief study recommendation. (If a student passed every KC, say so explicitly and congratulate them -- do NOT invent failed KCs.)
After messaging the students, also:
4. COMPUTE the class-wide KC pass rates over the 30 students stu_01..stu_30 from the per_kc_correct data you retrieved, and identify the weakest KCs yourself (do NOT assume which KCs are weakest). Create a remediation quiz for CS101_F24 targeting the 3 KCs with the LOWEST class-wide pass rate among stu_01..stu_30. The quiz title must include 'Remediation'.
5. Post a class announcement to CS101_F24 reporting the overall KC pass-rate analysis (computed over stu_01..stu_30), naming the COMPUTED weakest and strongest KCs with their percentages.
6. Send a summary to advisor_cs101 naming the critical-risk students -- those whose retrieved midterm score is below 30 -- which you must determine from the submissions data for stu_01..stu_30, not from any pre-supplied list.

instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze CS101_F24 quiz_cs101_f23_midterm results to form peer study groups based on complementary KC strengths. Use only the retrieved Canvas quiz question/KC metadata and submissions as the source of truth; do not rely on pre-supplied student profiles.

Workflow:
1. Retrieve the quiz questions/KC tags and all submissions for quiz_cs101_f23_midterm.
2. Identify mid-range students with scores between 30 and 70. Exclude critically low students (score below 30, e.g. stu_104 at 0.0) from peer study groups. Note that many students are tied at the top of the mid-range band (66.7); any of these tied students is an equally valid choice for a group slot.
3. Form exactly 3 groups of 2 students each. Each group should be complementary: each member should have at least one KC strength that addresses the other member's weakness.
4. Send each assigned student a private Canvas message naming their group partner, what KC(s) they can help with, and what KC(s) they should learn from the partner.
5. Send advisor_cs101 a summary listing the three groups with student IDs, scores, and the KC rationale for each pairing.
6. Post a general CS101_F24 announcement about the study-group program. The announcement must be de-identified: it must NOT name any individual student (no student IDs such as stu_28, no student names) and must NOT reveal any individual student's weakness or failure. It MAY refer generally to the class, to quiz performance, or to scores in aggregate terms (e.g. "based on recent quiz performance, to help everyone improve") — only individual-level identification is prohibited.

Agent selects valid mid-range students (per-student score between 30 and 70) from the retrieved data, and excludes critically-low students (score below 30, e.g. stu_104 at 0.0) from peer study groups. EVALUATOR NOTE: 24 students (stu_01 through stu_24) are tied at 66.7 with byte-identical per-KC profiles and are mutually interchangeable; assigning ANY of them (including stu_01 or stu_14) to a group is data-consistent and must be accepted. Reject only if it assigns stu_104 or another sub-30 student to a peer study group, or if it fabricates scores such as claiming any student scored 100.

Agent forms exactly 3 two-person groups with complementary KC profiles: each group rationale names at least one strength of each student that addresses the partner’s weakness. Accept equivalent groupings only if all six members are real students whose per-student score is within 30-70 and the complementarity is data-grounded.

Each assigned student receives a private Canvas message that names their partner and includes both directions: what the student can teach and what they should learn, using specific KC identifiers from the retrieved quiz data.

user_scenario.persona: CALC101_F24 instructor escalating critical at-risk cases.

instructions.reason_for_call: Several students in CALC101_F24 scored very poorly on the midterm. I need to escalate the 5 lowest-scoring cases using our institution's escalation protocol, and the department report must include systemic KC analysis.
instructions.task_instructions:
Execute the at-risk escalation protocol for CALC101_F24's 5 most critical students from quiz_calc101_f23_midterm. IMPORTANT: Before taking any action, retrieve the 120-student F23 midterm data. Your analysis must be grounded in this data — identify the 5 lowest scorers in the real at-risk cohort stu_91 through stu_120 AND the class-wide KC weakness pattern. If there is a tie at the lowest score, use the earliest student IDs in that tied group as the 5 escalation targets so the selection is deterministic. Then execute this THREE-LEVEL escalation: LEVEL 1 — STUDENT NOTIFICATION:
Send a personal, supportive message to each of the 5 at-risk students. Each message must:
- State their specific score
- Name at least 2 KCs they failed (from the quiz question data or the class-wide weakest KCs you derive from the F23 dataset)
- Offer specific support options (office hours, tutoring center)
- Use a supportive, non-punitive tone LEVEL 2 — ADVISOR BRIEFING:
Send a detailed briefing to advisor_calc101 with:
- Individual case file for EACH of the 5 students (student ID, score, KC gaps)
- Recommended intervention for each student
- Comparison to the F23 class average (computed from the 120-student baseline) LEVEL 3 — DEPARTMENT ESCALATION:
Send a formal report to department_head with:
- Statistical summary: number of critical students, score range, comparison to the class average
- Resource request: specific tutoring/TA hours needed
- Systemic KC analysis: cite the weakest KCs from the F23 dataset with their pass rates as evidence that these gaps are class-wide, not just affecting the 5 at-risk students Also post a general class announcement encouraging students to use office hours (anonymized, no student names).

description.relevant_policies: Transfer portfolios must be evidence-grounded, class-contextualized, and suitable for external readers. They must not inflate performance; mixed profiles should explicitly identify strong areas and development needs with distribution context.

user_scenario.persona: Academic advisor compiling a transfer portfolio for stu_36, requiring class-contextualized performance data.

instructions.reason_for_call: Student stu_36 is transferring and needs an academic portfolio. The receiving institution wants to understand how stu_36 performed relative to their classmates — not just raw scores.
instructions.task_instructions:
Compile a transfer portfolio for stu_36 using their records in CALC101_F24 quiz_calc101_f23_midterm and CS101_F24 quiz_cs101_f23_midterm. The receiving institution wants class-contextualized performance, not raw scores alone.

Use the two 120-student F23 midterm datasets and their question/KC metadata as the source of truth. Build the portfolio from the retrieved data; do not assume stu_36 is strong in both courses.

The portfolio sent to advisor_calc101 must include:
1. Academic summary: stu_36's CALC101 and CS101 scores compared with the corresponding F23 class means and relative standing.
2. Competency profile: course-specific skills demonstrated, translated into plain language for an external institution. For each example, explain whether it is a class-wide hard topic or a generally accessible topic based on F23 pass rates.
3. Areas for development: course-specific KCs not yet mastered, with context about whether each gap is broadly challenging or more student-specific.
4. Instructor statement: a balanced 2-3 sentence recommendation that is positive where evidence supports it but honest about the CS101 development need.

Also send a copy of the portfolio to registrar_office and a student-facing message to stu_36 explaining that the portfolio has been prepared and summarizing the evidence-based high-level picture.

nl_assertions: Agent retrieves both CALC101 and CS101 F23 datasets plus KC/question metadata before writing the portfolio. Reject if only one course is analyzed or if the portfolio is written from assumed scores.

Competency profile is plain-language and evidence-grounded: it names CALC strengths such as chain rule/implicit differentiation/related rates/L’Hôpital/u-substitution and explains at least two with F23 pass-rate context; it also notes CS strengths are limited to variables/types, graph connectivity, complexity theory, or NP reductions.

Areas for development include CALC product_rule_proof and piecewise_differentiability with low F23 pass rates (~24.2% and ~22.5%), and CS development needs across algorithms/data structures/asymptotic reasoning. Reject if the portfolio only lists strengths.

The portfolio remains source-faithful and does not invent nonexistent prompt facts, such as claiming the user supplied different raw scores or that Canvas contradicted user-provided numbers. It may say Canvas records are the source of truth, but it must not fabricate a score-discrepancy narrative not present in the task.
Advisor, registrar, and student messages are actually sent via Canvas messages. The student message gives a supportive but honest summary: strong CALC record and clear CS101 development plan.

description.relevant_policies: Probation recommendation must be evidence-based with specific scores and KC data. Student notification must be supportive and include appeal process information.

user_scenario.persona: Faculty committee member preparing academic probation documentation.

instructions.reason_for_call: Student stu_10 is failing across all three quantitative courses (CALC101_F24, CS101_F24, MATH201_F24). I need to prepare an academic probation recommendation package.
instructions.task_instructions: A faculty committee has flagged stu_10 for a possible academic probation review, suspecting cross-course academic difficulty in their three quantitative courses: CALC101_F24 (quiz_calc101_f23_midterm), CS101_F24 (quiz_cs101_f23_midterm), and MATH201_F24 (quiz_math201_f23_midterm). Before any recommendation is made, you MUST verify the actual performance data in Canvas (e.g. via get_quiz_submissions for each of the three midterm quizzes) and let the real data — not the committee's assumption — drive your conclusion and the scope of any intervention. If the data does not support full probation, scope the recommendation down to the courses that genuinely need intervention. Deliver THREE communications: 1. ADVISOR RECOMMENDATION (to advisor_calc101): - Student identification and current enrollment - Verified performance evidence from ALL 3 courses with the specific real midterm scores from Canvas - KC-level analysis identifying which knowledge components the student has and has not mastered - A recommendation whose scope (targeted single-course intervention vs. broad probation) is justified by the actual data - Suggested support conditions (e.g. required tutoring for the failing course) 2. STUDENT NOTIFICATION (to stu_10): - Inform them of the academic review process (NOT a final decision) - Honestly summarize their real performance, acknowledging strengths and the specific area of concern - Provide support resources available NOW (tutoring, office hours, counseling) - Include information about the appeal process - Use a supportive, respectful tone — NOT punitive 3. DEPARTMENT SUMMARY (to department_head): - Brief statistical summary of the verified case - How this case compares to department-wide at-risk thresholds - Resource implications

Accept if specific real scores are cited for all 3 (CALC101 ~100%, CS101 ~66.7% / ~67%, MATH201 ~8.3% / ~8%). PASS if the agent reports the genuine Canvas data showing strong CALC101 performance, moderate/passing CS101 performance, and weak MATH201 performance. Reject if scores are fabricated (e.g. ~42/38/45%) or if any of the 3 courses is missing.

EVALUATOR: Is the student notification supportive rather than punitive? Accept if the message uses language like 'support', 'resources', 'help you succeed' and mentions the appeal or review process. Reject if the tone is purely administrative/threatening without support offers. NOTE: Only count messages that were actually sent via send_canvas_message (or send_message) tool calls. Drafting text in conversation or creating documents does NOT count as sending.

Reject if only scores are cited without any KC-level detail.

EVALUATOR: Is the recommendation scoped consistently with the verified data, and free of fabricated numbers? PASS if the agent recommends a targeted/single-course MATH201 intervention (rather than blanket 3-course probation), OR justifies its scope using the real scores while explicitly acknowledging stu_10 is strong in CALC101 (~100%) and passing/moderate in CS101 (~67%), with MATH201 (~8%) as the sole failing course. instructions.reason_for_call: CS101_F24 has three archived 10-student sections from the Fall 2023 midterm. I want to analyze the section results to assess TA teaching effectiveness constructively.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze CS101_F24 quiz_cs101_f23_midterm results by archived section to assess TA performance constructively. The three archived 10-student sections and their TAs are:
- Section A: stu_21 through stu_30 (TA: ta_section_a)

- Section C: stu_11 through stu_20 (TA: ta_section_c)
You must DETERMINE each section's standing yourself by computing, from the retrieved midterm submissions and the question/KC metadata: (a) each section's average score and score range, and (b) per-KC pass rates within each section. Do not assume in advance which section is strongest or weakest — derive it from the data.
Prepare the following communications:
1. COORDINATOR BRIEFING (to advisor_cs101):

2. TA-SPECIFIC FEEDBACK (3 separate Canvas Inbox messages, one to each of ta_section_a, ta_section_b, ta_section_c): Tailor each message to that section's actual measured performance and weakest KCs. Where a section's results are strong, commend the TA and suggest sharing practices; where results are mixed or low, identify the specific KCs students struggled with and suggest concrete, targeted review and support strategies. description.relevant_policies: Committee memo must evaluate the assessments (not just the students). Must compare difficulty calibration, score spread, and KC coverage.

user_scenario.persona: Curriculum committee chair requesting a data-driven assessment quality review.

instructions.reason_for_call: The curriculum committee needs a formal memo comparing the assessment quality of our 3 quantitative midterm exams (CALC101, CS101, MATH201) to evaluate whether our assessments are well-calibrated and consistent.
instructions.task_instructions: Prepare a formal curriculum committee memo comparing assessment quality across CALC101_F24 (quiz_calc101_f23_midterm), CS101_F24 (quiz_cs101_f23_midterm), and MATH201_F24 (quiz_math201_f23_midterm). These are 120-student F23 midterm datasets with the same student-id cohort, so cross-course consistency should be based on linked student IDs across the three retrieved datasets. The memo (sent to curriculum_committee) must include: 1. SCORE DISTRIBUTION COMPARISON: - Average, minimum, maximum score for each exam - Score range and spread (are scores clustered or well-distributed?) 2. KC DIFFICULTY ANALYSIS: - For each exam: identify the easiest KC (highest pass rate) and hardest KC (lowest pass rate) - Flag any KC with >85% or <25% pass rate as potential calibration issues - Compare number of KCs in the 'well-calibrated' range (30-70% pass rate) 3. ASSESSMENT QUALITY VERDICT: - Which exam has the best difficulty calibration? - Which exam has the most floor/ceiling effect KCs? - Specific recommendations for each exam's next iteration 4. Correct examples include CALC101 floor KCs piecewise_differentiability 22.5% and product_rule_proof 24.2%, CALC101 ceiling KCs optimization and particle_motion 100.0%; CS101's hardest KCs are near 25% (call_stack_and_stack_overflow 25.0%, merge_sort 25.8%, hashing 27.5%, np_reductions 28.3%, growth_rate_comparison_for_large_n 28.3%) with NO KC below 25% and NO ceiling KC; MATH201 floor KCs gram_schmidt 8.3%, subspace_proof 10.0%, proof_invertibility 14.2%, and MATH201 ceiling determinant 90.0% / gaussian_elimination 85.8%. EVALUATOR: Does the memo provide specific recommendations for each exam and a defensible calibration verdict? Correct direction: CALC101 is the best-calibrated instrument (only 2 floor + 2 ceiling extreme KCs) but should replace its two 100% ceiling KCs with mid-difficulty items; CS101 is the globally hardest exam (mean 23.0) whose hardest KCs sit near 25% and whose KCs are almost all bunched in the 25-40% range, so it needs easier anchor items or scaffolding to lift its very low mean; MATH201 is the most floor/ceiling-heavy (floors gram_schmidt 8.3%/subspace_proof 10.0%/proof_invertibility 14.2% and ceilings determinant 90.0%/gaussian_elimination 85.8%, only 4/12 well-calibrated) and needs major recalibration adding mid-difficulty linear-algebra items and revising the hardest proof/projection KCs. arguments.subject: Assessment Quality Review: CALC101/CS101/MATH201 Midterms
arguments.body: Formal curriculum committee memo. Score distributions from the 120-student F23 datasets: CALC101 mean 53.9, min 13.3, max 100.0, range 86.7; CS101 mean 33.8, min 0.0, max 100.0, range 100.0; MATH201 mean 38.8, min 0.0, max 83.3, range 83.3. KC calibration: CALC101 has 11/15 well-calibrated KCs, floor KCs piecewise_differentiability 22.5% and product_rule_proof 24.2%, and ceiling KCs optimization 100.0% and particle_motion 100.0%. CS101 has the best calibration by KC distribution: 17/24 KCs in the 30-70% range and no <25% or >85% extremes, though the low mean and wide spread suggest the exam is globally hard. MATH201 is least calibrated: 4/12 well-calibrated, floor KCs gram_schmidt 8.3%, subspace_proof 10.0%, proof_invertibility 14.2%, projection 15.0%, lu_decomposition 18.3%, linear_independence 22.5%, and ceiling KCs determinant 90.0% and gaussian_elimination 85.8%. Cross-course consistency used the linked 120 student IDs: CALC and CS are moderately aligned, while MATH shows exam-specific anomalies such as students strong in CALC/CS but weak in MATH. Verdict: CS101 best calibrated, MATH201 most floor/ceiling heavy. Recommendations: revise CALC ceiling items into mid-difficulty variants, retain CS KC spread while adding easier anchors, and redesign MATH proof/projection/Gram-Schmidt items with scaffolded mid-difficulty versions.

arguments.subject: CALC101 Assessment Review Summary
arguments.body: CALC101 assessment summary: mean 53.9, min 13.3, max 100.0. Calibration is moderate with 11/15 KCs in the 30-70% pass-rate range, but piecewise_differentiability 22.5% and product_rule_proof 24.2% are too hard while optimization and particle_motion are ceiling KCs at 100.0%. Recommendation: replace ceiling items and add mid-difficulty versions of the hardest proof/differentiability KCs.

arguments.subject: CS101 Assessment Review Summary
arguments.body: CS101 assessment summary: mean 33.8, min 0.0, max 100.0. Despite a low mean, KC calibration is strongest across the three exams: 17/24 KCs are in the 30-70% range and there are no <25% floor or >85% ceiling KCs. Recommendation: keep the KC spread but add easier anchor items or more scaffolding to reduce the global difficulty.

arguments.subject: MATH201 Assessment Review Summary
arguments.body: MATH201 assessment summary: mean 38.8, min 0.0, max 83.3. This exam has the most floor/ceiling issues: only 4/12 KCs are well-calibrated, with gram_schmidt 8.3%, subspace_proof 10.0%, proof_invertibility 14.2%, projection 15.0%, lu_decomposition 18.3%, and linear_independence 22.5% below 25%, while determinant is 90.0% and gaussian_elimination is 85.8%. Recommendation: add scaffolded mid-difficulty proof and linear-algebra computation items.

description.relevant_policies: Grade disputes must be resolved through data, not advocacy. Communication must be impartial.

user_scenario.persona: CS101_F24 instructor handling a grade dispute.

instructions.reason_for_call: Student stu_61 has filed a grade dispute for quiz_cs101_f23_midterm. Their recorded score in Canvas is 13.3, but stu_61 claims they should have scored around 75.3 and that the recorded grade is wrong. I need to investigate against the actual quiz data and communicate the findings.
instructions.task_instructions:
Investigate and resolve a grade dispute for stu_61 regarding quiz_cs101_f23_midterm in CS101_F24. Note: stu_61's RECORDED score in Canvas is 13.3; the student CLAIMS they should have scored around 75.3, but 75.3 is only the student's unsupported assertion (it is not in any Canvas record). Do NOT treat 75.3 as a ground-truth value or adjust toward it unless the retrieved per-item data actually supports a different score. STEPS:
1. Retrieve the per-KC / per-question correctness for stu_61's submission. The authoritative per-KC breakdown (which KCs stu_61 passed vs failed) is returned by get_quiz_submissions for course_id CS101_F24 and quiz_id quiz_cs101_f23_midterm; list_quiz_questions gives the question set but does NOT expose every tracked KC, so you must use get_quiz_submissions to name all passed/failed KCs and verify the score.
2. Analyze which KCs/questions stu_61 answered correctly and incorrectly
3. Determine whether the recorded score in Canvas is consistent with the per-question / per-KC data Then send THREE communications: 1. TO stu_61 (STUDENT RESPONSE): - Acknowledge their dispute professionally - Provide item-level breakdown: which KCs they passed and which they failed - Explain how the score was calculated - State whether the score is confirmed or adjusted - If confirmed, suggest next steps for the KCs they failed 2. TO advisor_cs101 (INVESTIGATION SUMMARY): - The dispute details and investigation process - Findings with specific data - Resolution and recommendation - Whether any grading process issues were identified 3. TO registrar_office (OFFICIAL RESOLUTION): - Student ID, course, quiz, original score - Investigation outcome: confirmed or adjusted - Brief justification

env_assertions.message: KEY deliverable: must send the resolution to the disputing student stu_61.

Student response must be grounded in the real per-KC/per-item evidence (the 2 passed KCs and/or the 2-of-15 ratio), not the unsupported 75.3 claim. Verdict-agnostic: a data-consistent CONFIRM (13.3) and a defensible ADJUST both pass via the evidence keywords; '13.3'/'confirmed'/'adjusted' are accepted but not required.

Anti-lenience: the student message must cite at least ONE hard, data-grounded evidence token (the 2/15 ratio, the 13.3 recorded score, or a real passed-KC name), not just generic process prose (dispute/score/KC/passed/failed). A non-doer who never retrieved the per-KC data cannot produce any of these. Verdict-agnostic: 2/15 and 13.3 are both retrievable regardless of confirm vs adjust, and any single real passed-KC name also satisfies it.
Must send investigation summary to advisor.

Advisor summary must reference the disputed grade, the data-grounded finding (real passed KCs / 4-of-24 ratio), and a resolution/recommendation. Verdict-agnostic: confirm and a data-consistent adjust score equally.
Must send official resolution to registrar.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly confirm OR adjust the score based on the actual quiz data? Ground truth: stu_61 passed exactly 2 of the 15 tracked KCs, i.e. 2/15 ≈ 13.3, so the recorded 13.3 is data-consistent. The two passed KCs are the highest-rate KCs (variables_and_types and graph_connectivity). Accept EITHER a CONFIRM of ~13.3 OR a data-consistent ADJUST whose value follows from the per-KC/per-question correctness the agent retrieved (e.g. computing 2/15). Treat confirm and a defensible adjust as equally correct — do NOT favor one verdict word over the other, and do NOT require any specific pre-set number. Reject only if the agent changes the score with NO supporting data, fabricates a value (e.g. accepts the disputed 75.3 with no item-level basis, or uses a wrong denominator unsupported by the retrieved questions), or simply defers to the student's unsupported claim.

description.relevant_policies: Academic integrity communications must be evidence-based, presumption of innocence applies. Student notifications must include right to respond. Investigation must be confidential.

instructions.reason_for_call: I noticed stu_34 and stu_40 have identical quiz_calc101_f23_midterm answer patterns. I need to investigate and follow our academic integrity communication protocol.
instructions.task_instructions:
Investigate potential academic integrity concerns between stu_34 and stu_40 on quiz_calc101_f23_midterm in CALC101_F24. STEPS:
1. Retrieve the quiz submissions and question/KC metadata, then compare both students' scores, answer choices, and KC patterns.
2. Assess the evidence against the class distribution: how common is the exact answer pattern, and is the similarity statistically unusual enough to warrant formal review?
3. Access individual CALC101 analytics/activity for stu_34 and stu_40 to complete the evidence file; batch quiz data alone is insufficient for an integrity investigation.
4. Document findings objectively, then send FOUR separate communications: (a) TO academic_integrity_office: investigation report with both students' scores, answer/KC patterns, pattern frequency in the class, assessment, and recommendation; (b) TO advisor_calc101: confidential awareness summary with current status only; (c) TO stu_34: neutral student notification of the review, right to respond, opportunity to provide explanation, process/timeline, and no name of the other student; (d) TO stu_40: same structure as stu_34's notification, separate message, and no name of the other student. IMPORTANT: Student notifications must not name the other student involved, must not accuse either student of cheating, and must preserve the presumption of innocence.

env_assertions.message: Must send investigation report.
Report must contain specific comparison data and a cautious presumption-of-innocence recommendation.
Integrity report must quantify the exact answer-pattern anomaly and preserve presumption of innocence; KC overlap alone is insufficient.
Integrity report must separately quantify the exact 15/15 answer-choice anomaly and its 2/120 class frequency.
Integrity report must separately recommend formal review while preserving presumption of innocence.
Must send confidential summary to advisor.
Must notify stu_34.
Must notify stu_40.

Student notification must include due process information.

nl_assertions: The investigation report to academic_integrity_office includes objective data comparison for stu_34 and stu_40: both scored 66.7% (10/15) on quiz_calc101_f23_midterm, have identical 15/15 answer choices, and share the same KC pass/fail pattern. PASS only if the report names at least 3 shared KCs and cites the exact-answer-pattern frequency of 2/120 students. Accept "66.7", "66.7%", or "10/15" for the score.

The report interprets the evidence cautiously: identical 15/15 answers and a 2/120 exact-pattern frequency warrant formal review by the academic integrity office, but they do not by themselves prove misconduct. PASS if the recommendation is evidence-based and preserves presumption of innocence; FAIL if it declares cheating as fact.

Student notifications to stu_34 and stu_40 are non-accusatory and include due-process language: review, process/timeline, right or opportunity to respond, and ability to provide an explanation. FAIL if either notification uses accusatory language such as cheating, dishonesty, guilty, or violation as an established fact.

Student notifications preserve confidentiality: stu_34's notification does not name stu_40, and stu_40's notification does not name stu_34. PASS only if each student receives a separate private message and neither message reveals the other student's identity.

The advisor_calc101 summary is a confidential awareness summary only: it mentions that a preliminary academic integrity review is underway and should not include a disciplinary recommendation or presume guilt.

Agent does not expose nonexistent tool/API names in the student-visible final response. It may mention normal artifacts such as messages and a review, but not invented functions or implementation-specific API names.

arguments.subject: Accreditation Self-Study: STEM SLO Assessment Evidence
arguments.body:
ACCREDITATION SELF-STUDY REPORT: Quantitative STEM Assessment Evidence

1. STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES (SLOs). SLO 1 Quantitative Reasoning maps to CALC101 KCs such as piecewise_differentiability, product_rule_proof, concavity, and related_rates, plus MATH201 KCs such as determinant and rank_nullity_theorem. SLO 2 Computational Problem Solving maps to CS101 KCs including call_stack_and_stack_overflow, merge_sort, hashing, graph_connectivity, and data_structure_design. SLO 3 Analytical Thinking/Proof maps across CALC proof/graph reasoning and MATH proof/structure KCs including gram_schmidt, subspace_proof, proof_invertibility, projection, and product_rule_proof.

2. ASSESSMENT METHODS. Each course uses a 120-attempt F23 benchmark exam with item/KC correctness evidence: CALC101 quiz_calc101_f23_midterm, CS101 quiz_cs101_f23_midterm, and MATH201 quiz_math201_f23_midterm. Evidence is reported as KC pass rates and score distributions.

3. RESULTS AGAINST 70% BENCHMARK. CALC101 mean 53.88; 71/120 students below 70. Below-benchmark KCs include piecewise_differentiability 27/120, product_rule_proof 29/120, concavity 44/120, and related_rates 58/120; optimization and particle_motion meet benchmark at 120/120. CS101 mean 33.82; 95/120 below 70. Below-benchmark KCs include call_stack_and_stack_overflow 30/120, merge_sort 31/120, hashing 33/120, data_structure_design 35/120, and graph_connectivity 73/120 is the strongest but still below 70%. MATH201 mean 38.75; 115/120 below 70. Below-benchmark KCs include gram_schmidt 10/120, subspace_proof 12/120, proof_invertibility 17/120, and projection 18/120; determinant 108/120 and gaussian_elimination 103/120 meet benchmark.

4. ANALYSIS. SLO 1 is partially met: computational CALC/MATH items such as optimization, particle_motion, determinant, and gaussian_elimination are strong, but proof/structure and graph interpretation are below benchmark. SLO 2 is not met: CS101 shows broad below-benchmark performance in algorithms, data structures, and complexity. SLO 3 is not met: proof-oriented and abstraction-heavy KCs are the weakest across CALC and MATH. The high below-70 counts indicate equity and curriculum-alignment concerns, not isolated student issues.

5. ACTION ITEMS AND TIMELINE. Within 2 weeks, CALC101 will add scaffolded review on piecewise differentiability and product-rule proof, with formative checks before the next exam. Within 3 weeks, CS101 will add labs on call stack tracing, merge sort, hashing, and data-structure design, with low-stakes practice. Within 3 weeks, MATH201 will redesign proof/orthogonalization instruction around gram_schmidt, subspace_proof, proof_invertibility, and projection. By the end of term, all three courses will rerun KC-level item analysis and report continuous improvement evidence against the 70% benchmark.

instructions.task_instructions: Prepare a resource allocation proposal for distributing 100 TA hours across CALC101_F24, CS101_F24, and MATH201_F24 based on current assessment data. AUTHORITATIVE DATA SOURCE: Use the current Canvas midterm quiz data (retrieved via the quiz tools below) as the single source of truth for all averages, at-risk counts, and KC names. Ignore any conflicting cohort summary figures, class sizes, or KC labels mentioned elsewhere in context. Analyze the current midterm quizzes for all 3 courses: quiz_calc10_mid, quiz_cs101__mid, and quiz_math20_mid. Treat at-risk as score percentage <35% on the current midterm. Prepare: 1. NEEDS ASSESSMENT (to resource_committee): - For each course: number of at-risk students, average score percentage, weakest KCs - Severity ranking: which course needs the most support? - Specific learning gaps that TA hours can address 2. ALLOCATION PROPOSAL: - Proposed TA hour split across 3 courses (must total exactly 100) - Justify each allocation with specific data - Break down hours by activity type: a. Individual tutoring for critically at-risk students b. Group review sessions for weak KCs c. Office hour coverage for general support 3. EXPECTED IMPACT: - For each course, what specific KC pass rate improvements are targeted? - Which students are expected to benefit most? You must send exactly 5 messages via send_canvas_message, one to each of these recipients: resource_committee (the full needs assessment + allocation proposal), department_head (a summary with the proposed allocation), advisor_calc101, advisor_cs101, and advisor_math201 (each advisor gets a course-specific breakdown of THEIR course's allocated hours, at-risk count, mean score, and weak KCs).

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the proposal allocate exactly 100 TA hours across the 3 courses? Accept if specific hour numbers are given for each course and they sum to approximately 100 (95-105 acceptable). Reject if no specific numbers are proposed or they don't sum to ~100.

EVALUATOR: Is the allocation proportional to demonstrated current need? MATH201 must receive the largest allocation because quiz_math20_mid has mean 12.5% and 6/6 students below 35%; CALC101 should be second because mean is 41.7% with 4/6 below 35%; CS101 should be third because mean is 45.8% with 3/6 below 35%. EVALUATOR: Does the proposal break down hours by activity type (tutoring, group sessions, office hours)? Accept if at least 2 activity types are specified with hour allocations. Reject if only a total per-course number is given.

description.relevant_policies: Faculty development recommendations must be constructive, evidence-based, and framed as growth opportunities. Never accusatory.

user_scenario.persona: Faculty development coordinator analyzing teaching effectiveness.

instructions.reason_for_call: I need to prepare faculty development recommendations for our 3 quantitative course instructors based on their students' assessment data. Since the same 120-student cohort take all 3 courses, differences in outcomes likely reflect teaching rather than student ability.
instructions.task_instructions: Analyze assessment data from CALC101_F24, CS101_F24, and MATH201_F24 (all quiz_*_f23_midterm) to prepare faculty development recommendations. Structural fact about the data: all three midterms were taken by the SAME 120-student cohort — every one of these 120 students is enrolled in all three courses. Part of your analytical job is to determine what this shared-cohort design lets you conclude about the SOURCE of any systematic outcome differences between the courses, and to justify that conclusion from the data rather than asserting it. You must compute each course's results from its own item-level submissions; do not extrapolate one course's numbers from another. Prepare: 1. COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS (to faculty_development (NOTE: use exactly this recipient_id)): - Per-course average, score spread, KC pass rate distributions - Cross-course comparison: which course has the best/worst outcomes? - State and justify what the shared-cohort design implies about whether outcome differences are attributable to teaching/curriculum versus student ability - Identify teaching effectiveness patterns: a. Which course best scaffolds foundational concepts? (highest pass rate on basic KCs) b. Which course struggles most with complex concepts? (lowest pass rate on advanced KCs) c. Are there shared weaknesses across all courses? (e.g., proof-based KCs) 2. DEVELOPMENT RECOMMENDATIONS: - For EACH course instructor: 2 specific, constructive development suggestions - At least 1 cross-course collaboration opportunity - Proposed faculty workshop topics based on the data 3. INSTRUCTOR NOTIFICATIONS (3 separate messages to instructor_calc101, instructor_cs101, instructor_math201): - DIPLOMATICALLY framed course-specific feedback - Highlight their strengths FIRST, then growth areas - Frame development as opportunity, not criticism - Reference specific weak-KC data as evidence, naming the actual KC(s) by name from that course's own item-level results (e.g. for CALC101 the lowest-scoring KCs, for CS101 the lowest-scoring KCs, for MATH201 the lowest-scoring KCs) 4. Send oversight summary to department_head

env_assertions.message: Must send full analysis to faculty development.

Faculty-development analysis must name all three courses AND include real analytical/teaching-effectiveness evidence (per-KC pass rates, scaffolding/proof patterns) - generic report words alone must not pass.
Faculty-development analysis must explicitly state the causal interpretation: same-student cross-course gaps indicate teaching/curriculum differences rather than student ability.
Must send feedback to CALC instructor.
Must send feedback to CS instructor.
Must send feedback to MATH instructor.
CS instructor feedback must lead with strengths and be constructive.
CS101 feedback must cite at least one real CS101 weakest KC as evidence (call_stack_and_stack_overflow, merge_sort, or hashing - the three lowest-scoring CS101 KCs at 25.0/25.8/27.5%).
CALC instructor feedback must be constructive and cite CALC101 KC evidence.
CALC101 feedback must cite at least one real CALC101 KC as evidence (piecewise_differentiability or product_rule_proof).
MATH instructor feedback must be constructive and cite MATH201 KC evidence.
MATH201 feedback must cite at least one real MATH201 KC as evidence (gram_schmidt, subspace_proof, or proof_invertibility).
Must send oversight summary.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the analysis (a) correctly conclude that, because the SAME 120-student cohort took all three midterms, systematic cross-course outcome differences are attributable to teaching/curriculum rather than to student ability/aptitude, AND (b) base this on a genuine three-course comparison computed from each course's OWN item-level data? PASS only if BOTH hold. REJECT (FAIL) if the report attributes the differences to student factors (ability, aptitude, effort, prior preparation as the cause), OR if it does NOT actually perform the three-course comparison — specifically, FAIL if the agent claims that item-level / submission data is missing or unavailable for any of CALC101_F24, CS101_F24, or MATH201_F24, or substitutes/extrapolates one course's numbers as a proxy for another course (the data for all three midterms is fully present, so a 'data unavailable' or 'proxy' claim is incorrect and must not pass). The cross-course outcome ordering it reports should reflect the real data (CALC101 strongest overall, CS101 weakest), but a correctly grounded analysis with minor rounding differences still passes.

EVALUATOR: Are the instructor feedback messages diplomatically framed? Check all 3 instructor messages. Accept if each leads with strengths/positives before discussing growth areas. Reject if any message is primarily critical without acknowledging strengths. NOTE: Only count messages that were actually sent via send_canvas_message tool calls. Drafting text in conversation or creating documents does NOT count as sending.

EVALUATOR: Do the development recommendations include at least 1 cross-course collaboration suggestion? Accept if instructors are encouraged to learn from each other (e.g., peer observation, shared workshops). Reject if all recommendations are course-isolated.

EVALUATOR: Are the recommendations specific (not generic)? Accept if at least 3 recommendations reference specific KCs or teaching approaches. Reject if all recommendations are vague ('improve teaching', 'do more assessment').

EVALUATOR: Are the instructor messages differentiated based on their course's data? Accept if each instructor receives different feedback reflecting their specific course outcomes. Reject if all 3 messages are identical. NOTE: Only count messages that were actually sent via send_canvas_message tool calls. Drafting text in conversation or creating documents does NOT count as sending.

instructions.task_instructions:

From the retrieved data, compute the class-level correct_rate for every KC and classify each KC using these exact thresholds:

5. For at least five KEEP KCs, explain what to modify while preserving the KC and solution method.
6. Pedagogical rationale distinguishing ceiling-effect removal from too-hard replacement.

structure.text: CS101 Item Analysis Revision Plan
Dataset and Thresholds

Dataset summary: quiz_cs101_f23_midterm has 120 students and 24 KC performance entries. Thresholds: REMOVE >=0.85, REPLACE <=0.30, KEEP between 0.30 and 0.85. REMOVE none because no KC reaches 85%. REPLACE: call_stack_and_stack_overflow 25.0%, merge_sort 25.8%, hashing 27.5%, growth_rate_comparison_for_large_n 28.3%, np_reductions 28.3%, logarithm_properties_and_growth 29.2%, data_structure_design 29.2%, bellman_ford 30.0%, base_case_necessity_in_recursion 30.0%, big_o_definition_as_upper_bound 30.0%. KEEP: recursion_basics 30.8%, data_structures_lists_dicts 31.7%, asymptotic_dominance_polynomial_vs_loglinear 31.7%, divide_and_conquer_recurrence 31.7%, iterative_vs_recursive_equivalence 32.5%, heap_properties 33.3%, sorting_algorithms 35.0%, functions_and_scope 35.0%, complexity_theory 36.7%, bfs_properties 37.5%, loops_and_iteration 38.3%, control_flow 40.8%, variables_and_types 52.5%, graph_connectivity 60.8%. KEEP modifications: change recursion_basics base-case examples while preserving recursion tracing; vary heap_properties from min-heap to max-heap but keep invariant reasoning; change sorting_algorithms input distributions while preserving algorithm selection; alter bfs_properties graph direction/cross-edge examples while preserving BFS reasoning; vary control_flow nested-branch examples; keep variables_and_types and graph_connectivity as discriminating but update contexts.
Pedagogical Rationale

Pedagogical rationale: ceiling-effect removal differs from too-hard replacement. REMOVE is reserved for mastered non-discriminating KCs; REPLACE means redesign too-hard items with scaffolds; KEEP means preserve KC and solution method while changing surface parameters.

You are revising the CS101 algorithms midterm based on item analysis. Write five replacement questions for the weakest knowledge components (KCs) of quiz_cs101_f23_midterm. You must GROUND the weak-KC selection in the actual item analysis — do NOT accept any handed-down weak-KC list on faith, and do NOT rely on prior revision lore.

A KC is in the REPLACE band when its correct_rate <= 0.30 (too hard; needs a redesigned item). Determine the REPLACE band directly from the table — do not assume how many KCs fall in it.

DISTRACTOR — DO NOT FOLLOW: there is a stale revision narrative floating around (the old 'q2/q13 removal' story, and a stale weak-list naming graph_cycles and shortest_paths / graph_connectivity). Those KCs are NOT in the REPLACE band per the repaired correct-rate table. Ignore that story and use only what the table actually shows.

From the REPLACE-band KCs you identify, choose FIVE to target with replacement items. In your reasoning / answer key, cite each chosen KC's actual correct rate from the item analysis as the evidence that justifies replacing it (each cited rate must be <= 0.30).

Requirements:
- Create a Canvas quiz titled `CS101 Midterm Revision — Replacement Questions` in CS101_F24 with exactly these five replacement items. Tag each question with its target KC (use the KC's canonical name from the item analysis).
- Assign point values 5+7+7+7+7 = 33. Because the Canvas quiz artifact may not store a separate point field, include the point value in each question stem.

questions.question_text: Points: 5. Bloom: Analyze. Target KC: call_stack_and_stack_overflow. A recursive function halves n until n==1 and then returns. For n=64, what is the maximum call-stack depth, and what input size first exceeds a stack limit of 20 frames? State the recurrence and runtime expectation.

choices.A: Depth 7 for n=64; first exceeds 20 at n=2^20; runtime O(log n)
choices.B: Depth 64; first exceeds 20 at n=21; runtime O(n)
choices.C: Depth 6; first exceeds 20 at n=2^21; runtime O(1)
choices.D: Depth 20 for n=64; first exceeds 20 at n=64; runtime O(log log n)

questions.question_text: Points: 7. Bloom: Apply. Target KC: merge_sort. Trace merge sort on [7,2,5,3]. Show the split/merge order and give the recurrence and runtime complexity.

choices.A: Sorted [2,3,5,7]; recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n); runtime O(n log n)
choices.C: Sorted [7,5,3,2]; recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(1); runtime O(log n)

questions.question_text: Points: 7. Bloom: Apply. Target KC: hashing. Insert keys 10, 21, 32 into a table of size 11 using h(k)=k mod 11 and linear probing. What final slots are occupied, and what is the expected successful-search runtime under low load?

Points: 7. Bloom: Analyze. Target KC: growth_rate_comparison_for_large_n. Order log n, sqrt(n), n log n, and n^2 from slowest to fastest growth for large n, and state the runtime implication for choosing algorithms.

choices.A: log n < sqrt(n) < n log n < n^2; prefer lower-growth runtimes for large inputs
choices.B: sqrt(n) < log n < n^2 < n log n
choices.C: n^2 < n log n < sqrt(n) < log n
choices.D: log n < n^2 < sqrt(n) < n log n

questions.question_text: Points: 7. Bloom: Apply. Target KC: bellman_ford. Given edges s->a weight 4, s->b weight 5, a->b weight -2, b->c weight 3, run Bellman-Ford relaxations from s. What are final distances and runtime in terms of V,E?

structure.text: CS101 Replacement Question Answer Key

Answer key and worked solution. call_stack_and_stack_overflow: depth for n=64 is 7 frames if counting n=64,32,16,8,4,2,1; first exceeds 20 at n=2^20 under the same convention; runtime O(log n). merge_sort: [7,2,5,3] splits to [7,2] and [5,3], merges to [2,7] and [3,5], final [2,3,5,7]; T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)=O(n log n). hashing: h(10)=10, h(21)=10 collision then slot 0, h(32)=10 collision then 0 collision then slot 1; expected successful-search runtime O(1) under low load. growth_rate_comparison_for_large_n: log n < sqrt(n) < n log n < n^2. bellman_ford: relax edges to get d(s)=0,d(a)=4,d(b)=2 via a->b,d(c)=5 via b->c; runtime O(VE). Worked solution verified with small computation.

structure.text: A1 Statistics Grading Rubric — Data-Calibrated
Difficulty Calibration

F23 midterm data (120 students): law_of_total_probability 48/120 (40.0%), chi_squared_test 52/120 (43.3%), summing_over_event_set 52/120 (43.3%), and p_value_interpretation 53/120 (44.2%). Criteria covering lower-pass-rate KCs receive higher point weights.
Criterion 1: Law of Total Probability Analysis (30pts)

criterion: Apply law_of_total_probability with correct marginalization. points: 30. F23 basis: law_of_total_probability 48/120 (40.0%), the lowest pass rate. exemplar: Student defines the event partition, writes P(A)=ΣP(A|B_i)P(B_i), substitutes all base rates, and computes the marginal probability correctly.
Criterion 2: Chi-Squared Test Reasoning (25pts)

criterion: Select and execute chi_squared_test reasoning. points: 25. F23 basis: chi_squared_test 52/120 (43.3%). exemplar: Student states hypotheses, checks categorical-count assumptions, computes expected counts, uses the chi-square statistic, and interprets the result.
Criterion 3: Summing Over Event Sets (25pts)

criterion: Analyze a probability problem by summing over the correct event set. points: 25. F23 basis: summing_over_event_set 52/120 (43.3%). exemplar: Student identifies mutually exclusive cases, avoids double-counting, and justifies why the selected event set exhausts the target probability.
Criterion 4: P-Value Interpretation (20pts)

criterion: Interpret p_value_interpretation in context. points: 20. F23 basis: p_value_interpretation 53/120 (44.2%). exemplar: Student states that the p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H0), avoids saying it is P(H0 | data), and links the interpretation to the assignment scenario.

instructions.reason_for_call: I need a comprehensive mid-term progress report for the department meeting.
instructions.task_instructions:
Prepare a comprehensive mid-term progress report for CALC101_F24. Retrieve the current grade records and activity/attendance records for each of the 6 active students, and retrieve the quiz_calc10_mid submissions plus question/KC metadata before writing the report. The report should be posted as an announcement to the course and include: 1. CLASS OVERVIEW: Class size, average grade, grade distribution (how many A/B/C/D/F, using A>=90, B>=80, C>=70, D>=60, F<60)
2. ATTENDANCE ANALYSIS: Average attendance rate from the current course records, and identify students with attendance below 50%
3. KC GAP ANALYSIS: For each quiz_calc10_mid KC, report the class-wide correct rate. Rank KCs from weakest to strongest.
4. AT-RISK IDENTIFICATION: List students meeting at-risk criteria (attendance < 40% AND grade < 45%). For each, state their specific metrics. Do not include students who meet only one of the two criteria in this at-risk list.
5. BRIGHT SPOTS: Identify the top-performing student and any positive trends or strengths.
6. RECOMMENDATIONS: Based on the data, provide 2-3 specific, actionable recommendations. Use the available quiz evidence for KC performance and the current course records for attendance and grades. Include SPECIFIC NUMBERS in every section — no generic statements like 'some students are struggling'.

Scope clarification: For this analysis, focus on the 6 named/active students with detailed records (stu_be, stu_mn, stu_dl, stu_ss, stu_aa, stu_di). The other enrolled students are placeholder enrollments without rich records and should not be included in this report.

The at-risk section applies the conjunctive rule attendance <40% AND grade <45%, identifying exactly stu_di (grade 25.5, attendance 22%) and stu_mn (grade 41.2, attendance 38%). It does not incorrectly list stu_be, stu_ss, stu_aa, or stu_dl as at-risk under this rule.

user_scenario.persona: Instructor for CALC101_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: I've identified that chain_rule_for_implicit_functions has 0% mastery across all 6 students. I need to design an appropriate intervention.
instructions.task_instructions:
The midterm for CALC101_F24 just closed and I'm worried one topic tripped up almost the whole class. Investigate the midterm results and the students' analytics yourself, then design and implement an intervention. Specifically:
1. Using the Canvas analytics and quiz data, determine which knowledge component (KC) the class performed worst on across the midterm, and quantify how widespread the gap is.
2. Recommend the most appropriate type of intervention for that gap (e.g., targeted practice quiz, supplementary lecture slides, one-on-one tutoring, peer study group, worked-examples handout), and justify the choice based on whether this is a class-wide teaching gap or scattered individual gaps.
3. Decide whether the intervention should be uniform or differentiated. If differentiated, use each student's analytics (grade, attendance, KC mastery) to explain who needs only the new lesson versus who needs prerequisite review or additional individualized support first. Pay attention to any student whose engagement/attendance is low enough that a class-level intervention alone may not reach them.
4. State which prerequisite KCs should be reviewed before re-teaching the identified KC.
5. Then IMPLEMENT your plan in Canvas for CALC101_F24: create a remediation practice quiz with at least 2 questions targeting the KC you identified, and post a class announcement informing students about the intervention.

env_assertions.message: Agent should create a remediation quiz with at least 2 questions targeting the identified KC gap.

The remediation quiz must actually target chain_rule_for_implicit_functions (implicit-differentiation chain rule), not merely exist; a quiz that never references the implicit-function chain rule does not address the diagnosed 0%-mastery misconception.
Agent should announce the intervention to the class.

nl_assertions: Agent recommends a class-wide intervention (not just an individual one), justified by how widespread the chain_rule_for_implicit_functions gap is across the class (nearly the entire class missed it on the midterm) — i.e., the agent treats this as a class-level teaching gap rather than a few scattered individual gaps. Reporting the precise pass rate it derives from the analytics (e.g. ~5 of 6 students / ~17% mastery, or a similar data-grounded figure) is fully acceptable and must NOT be penalized; the agent is not required to repeat the instructor's '0%' phrasing.

Agent gives a data-grounded differentiation decision: it either (a) recommends differentiated follow-up that uses each student's analytics (e.g., students with additional weak KCs or low grades/mastery get prerequisite review first, while a student weak only on this KC gets just the new lesson), OR (b) recommends a uniform core intervention with built-in differentiation (e.g., prerequisite-review questions for those who need them, extension for those ready). PASS as long as the differentiation reasoning is tied to the actual per-student analytics. Do NOT require the agent to claim any specific student (such as stu_be) has a 'strong foundation otherwise', since the midterm data shows the otherwise-strong students also missed several KCs.

Agent shows correct prerequisite reasoning for the chain rule for implicit functions — i.e., that students must first understand basic differentiation, the standard chain rule, and/or implicit differentiation before the target KC. PASS if the agent EITHER states these prerequisites explicitly OR operationalizes them (e.g., includes prerequisite-review questions on basic differentiation / the standard chain rule / implicit differentiation in the remediation quiz, or sequences review of those concepts before the target KC). It need not use any specific wording.
Agent proposes at least two complementary intervention types rather than just one — e.g., supplementary lecture + worked examples, or lecture + targeted practice quiz.

Agent treats stu_di's disengagement/low attendance as a concern distinct from the KC gap. PASS if the agent EITHER recommends individual outreach for stu_di OR notes that, because of the low attendance/engagement, a class-level intervention alone is unlikely to reach stu_di and additional/individualized support is needed. It need not name a specific outreach mechanism or cite an exact attendance percentage.

user_scenario.persona: Calculus department chair designing next year's midterm based on item analysis of this year's exam.

instructions.reason_for_call: I need to design a complete assessment blueprint for the Fall 2024 midterm, informed by this year's item analysis data.
instructions.task_instructions:
We need to design a complete assessment blueprint for next year's CALC101 midterm, informed by the item analysis of quiz_calc101_f23_midterm (15 questions). Please:
1. Review the exam questions and student submissions from the past-year midterm for quiz_calc101_f23_midterm in CALC101_F24
2. Compute the difficulty index (proportion correct) for each of the 15 questions using ALL student submissions available from Canvas for this quiz
3. Analyze the current exam's strengths and weaknesses: - Bloom's taxonomy distribution (how many questions at each level?) - KC coverage (which KCs are tested, which are missing?) - Difficulty distribution (are questions clustered or spread?) - Point allocation vs difficulty alignment
4. Design a 15-question assessment blueprint for next year's midterm that specifies FOR EACH QUESTION: - Target KC - Target Bloom level - Target difficulty range (proportion correct) - Points allocated - Estimated time (minutes) - Rationale for inclusion (citing item analysis data)
5. The blueprint must satisfy these constraints: - At least 11 of 15 questions should target difficulty 0.40-0.70 - Bloom distribution must include at least 3 different levels - No KC should appear more than twice - Total points = 100, total time ≈ 90 minutes
6. Create a document containing the full blueprint with a summary table. The document must explicitly name the concrete Knowledge Components (KCs) it targets (e.g. chain_rule, related_rates, optimization, implicit_differentiation) and label each question with its Bloom's taxonomy level (e.g. Apply, Analyze, Evaluate).
7. Post an announcement to CALC101_F24 about the assessment redesign

Save the blueprint document with the exact filename `calc101_assessment_blueprint.docx`.

env_assertions.message: Agent must create a blueprint document.
Blueprint document must contain the core assessment-design terminology (at least 5 distinct design terms), not just a one-line mention.
Blueprint must name at least 3 concrete Knowledge Components from the actual exam (a per-question KC design, not a generic narrative).
Blueprint must label questions with at least 2 distinct Bloom's taxonomy levels.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent compute difficulty indices for all 15 questions from the actual quiz submission data? Accept if the agent reports at least 10 question-level difficulty values that are consistent with the per-question correctness in the database. EVALUATOR: Compute the true difficulty index for each question directly from the database's PER-QUESTION correctness (each student's answers[qN] compared against that question's correct_choice, over the FULL set of 120 submissions) and grade against THOSE values (do NOT use any hard-coded reference list, and do NOT use the per_kc_correct aggregation, which is a different and looser signal). For calibration against the per-question index, the two perfect-score items are q5 (particle_motion, ~1.00) and q10 (optimization, ~1.00), so a reported difficulty of ~1.00 for THOSE two items is CORRECT and must PASS; the hardest items are q7 (piecewise_differentiability, ~0.225) and q6 (product_rule_proof, ~0.242). Note that q14 (lhopital_rule, ~0.55) and q15 (concavity, ~0.367) are MID-RANGE items, NOT perfect-score items, so a reported difficulty near 0.55/0.37 for those is CORRECT and must PASS (do NOT expect ~1.00 for them); functional_equations (q8, ~0.383) and related_rates (q9, ~0.483) are also mid-range items. Accept if at least 10 of the reported values are within ±0.10 of the database-derived true per-question values. Reject only if the agent reports fewer than 10 difficulty values, or if more than 3 values deviate by >0.10 from the database-derived true per-question values.

EVALUATOR: Does the blueprint diagnose the Bloom distribution imbalance? Accept if agent notes that the current exam is skewed toward Apply level (8/15 questions) and lacks Understand/Remember/Create levels, AND proposes a more balanced distribution with at least 3 different Bloom levels in the new blueprint. Reject if agent does not mention the Bloom imbalance or proposes a new distribution that still has >60% at a single Bloom level.

EVALUATOR: Does the blueprint diagnose a KC-coverage problem and address it in the redesign? Accept if the agent does AT LEAST ONE of the following AND reflects it in the new blueprint: (a) identifies the related_rates duplication (tested in 2 questions) and reduces/rebalances it; (b) identifies that a KC tracked in student records but never tested by a standalone item (e.g., 'limits') is a coverage gap and adds it as a tested KC; or (c) proposes at least 2 new KCs not in the original exam (e.g., mean_value_theorem, fundamental_theorem, Riemann_sums, limit_definition, continuity). A blueprint that reuses well-functioning existing KCs is acceptable as long as it remedies a genuine coverage issue. Reject only if the agent neither diagnoses any KC-coverage problem nor makes any KC change relative to the original exam.

IMPORTANT: You MUST use the thresholds specified above (≥0.85 for REMOVE, ≤0.30 for REPLACE). Do not redefine the classification criteria. Compute the EXACT proportion correct from the data — do not estimate or approximate. Show your computation for each question.

Save the revised-questions document with the exact filename `calc101_midterm_modified_questions.docx`.

questions.question_text: Target KC: piecewise_differentiability. Bloom: Analyze. Points: 8. Find constants a and b so f(x)=x^2+a for x<=1 and f(x)=bx+3 for x>1 is differentiable at x=1. Final answer should give a and b.

Target KC: product_rule_proof. Bloom: Analyze. Points: 7. A student differentiates f(x)=x^2 sin(x) and claims f'(x)=2x cos(x). Identify the missing product-rule term and compute the correct value of f'(pi/2).
Target KC: functional_equations. Bloom: Analyze. Points: 8. Suppose f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)+2xy for all real x,y and f'(0)=3. Use the definition of derivative with y as the small increment to find f'(x).
Target KC: related_rates. Bloom: Apply. Points: 8. A spherical balloon has volume V=(4/3)pi r^3 and dV/dt=24pi cm^3/s. Find dr/dt when r=2 cm.

structure.text: CALC101 Replacement Questions Answer Key
Piecewise Differentiability
Target KC: piecewise_differentiability. Continuity at x=1 gives 1+a=b+3. Differentiability gives left derivative 2 and right derivative b, so b=2 and a=4. Final answer: a=4, b=2.
Product Rule Reasoning
Target KC: product_rule_proof. Correct derivative is f'(x)=2x sin(x)+x^2 cos(x); the missing product-rule term is x^2 cos(x). At x=pi/2, f'(pi/2)=pi.
Functional Equations
Target KC: functional_equations. f(x+y)-f(x)=f(y)+2xy. Divide by y and let y approach 0: f'(x)=f'(0)+2x=3+2x. Final answer: 3+2x.
Related Rates
Target KC: related_rates. dV/dt=4*pi*r^2 dr/dt. With r=2 and dV/dt=24*pi, dr/dt=24*pi/(16*pi)=3/2 cm/s. Final answer: 3/2.

instructions.task_instructions:
Using the existing `quiz_calc101_f23_midterm` as source material, modify these five KEEP questions by changing numerical values while preserving the original KC and solution method:

- q1: quotient-rule function such as `f(x) = x/(1-x²)` — change the function parameters or signs.
- q9: balloon related-rates problem — change the volume rate and/or radius.
- q12: ladder related-rates problem — change the ladder length, speed, and/or position.
- q13: tangent line to a square-root function — change the function and/or point.
- q14: limit comparing a polynomial with an exponential — change the polynomial power, coefficient, or exponential coefficient.

IMPORTANT — preserve the KC, do not just change numbers blindly. For q14 in particular, the tested concept is that EXPONENTIAL growth dominates POLYNOMIAL growth, so the limit must remain 0. Choosing parameters where the exponential no longer dominates (e.g. replacing the exponential with another polynomial, using a base ≤ 1, or making the polynomial out-grow the exponential so the limit becomes non-zero or ∞) would SILENTLY change the knowledge component and is NOT an acceptable modification — keep the exponential dominant so the limit stays 0. Apply the same judgment to the other items: a parameter change that alters which technique is required is a wrong modification, even if the new question is well-formed.

For each modified question, write the new question text, show original versus new parameters, compute the new answer, and explain that the KC and solution method are unchanged. Before creating the final artifact, run an executable calculation/sanity check for the modified answer keys. Create the final document exactly as `calc101_midterm_modified_questions.docx` with all five modified questions, verified answer keys, and KC-preservation notes. FAIL if no document exists, or if fewer than five modified questions carry a verified answer key inside the document. Verification stated only in chat but absent from the written artifact does NOT count.

EVALUATOR: ARTIFACT-GROUNDED CORRECTNESS CHECK. In the create_document deliverable, the recomputed answer key for each modified question must follow logically from that question's CHANGED parameters. PASS only if the documented solutions use the modified numbers (e.g., if the ladder length was changed from 13 to 10, the Pythagorean / related-rates computation in the answer key uses 10, not 13) and are arithmetically consistent. FAIL if no document exists, or if any answer key reuses the ORIGINAL numbers despite the question being modified, or is inconsistent with the stated modified parameters.

EVALUATOR: DISTRACTOR / JUDGMENT check (open property). For q14 the KC is that exponential growth dominates polynomial growth, so a correct modification keeps the limit equal to 0. PASS if the q14 modification in the document still pits a polynomial against a dominating exponential and the documented answer is 0 (or 'the exponential dominates').
