arguments.new_body:
Formal decomposition (squared-error loss):
  E[(y − f̂(x))²] = Bias[f̂(x)]² + Var[f̂(x)] + σ²_noise
   • Bias  = E[f̂(x)] − f_true(x)   → systematic error from model assumptions
   • Var   = E[(f̂(x) − E[f̂(x)])²] → sensitivity to the particular training sample
   • σ²    = irreducible noise (a lower bound; no model can beat it)

Diagnosing overfitting (operational signals, not just intuition):
  1. Train error LOW and validation error HIGH → high variance / overfit
  2. Train error HIGH and validation error HIGH and close → high bias / underfit
  3. Learning curve: validation loss decreases then RISES while training loss keeps falling
  4. Large gap between training and validation metric that grows with model complexity

Worked numerical intuition:
  Suppose Bias² = 0.1, Var = 0.6, σ² = 0.05 → expected loss = 0.75; reducing variance to 0.2 (e.g., via regularisation) at the cost of Bias² rising to 0.15 yields loss = 0.40 — a net win.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Targets KCs: bias_variance_tradeoff_formal and overfitting_definition_and_diagnosis (both flagged weak on the Week-5 midterm quiz; 4/6 and 2/6 students missed these respectively). Walk class through the decomposition term-by-term on the board, then demo the learning-curve diagnostic on the polynomial regression notebook. Emphasise that "overfitting" is defined by the train–validation GAP, not by absolute training accuracy.
arguments.new_title: Bias–Variance Tradeoff (formal) & Overfitting Diagnosis

arguments.new_body:
Why regularisation reduces VARIANCE (not just "shrinks weights"):
  • Unregularised OLS solution: ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy — can be ill-conditioned, weights swing wildly across resamples → HIGH VARIANCE
  • Ridge (L2): ŵ = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy — adding λI stabilises the inverse, so weight estimates change LESS from sample to sample → variance ↓
  • L1 (Lasso): non-differentiable penalty drives some weights exactly to 0 → simpler effective model, lower variance, automatic feature selection

The bias–variance trade you are explicitly making:
  λ = 0      → Bias low,  Variance HIGH (overfit)
  λ → ∞     → Bias HIGH, Variance ≈ 0 (underfit, predicts the mean)
  optimal λ → minimises Bias² + Variance on validation data (chosen by k-fold CV)

Common student misconception (addressed):
  "Regularisation prevents overfitting by making the model smaller." 
  More precisely: regularisation constrains the HYPOTHESIS SPACE, which reduces the variance of the estimator — that is *how* it mitigates overfitting. Smaller weights are a symptom, not the mechanism.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Targets KC: regularization_as_variance_reduction (4/6 students missed this on the Week-5 midterm quiz). Spend extra time on the (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹ stability argument — last cohort's confusion was treating regularisation as a magic "shrink" rather than as variance control. Tie back to the bias–variance decomposition slide so students see λ as a knob that trades the two terms.

bullets: Wrong intuition: 'high training accuracy = overfitting'
Right intuition: train error LOW + validation error HIGH = overfitting
Learning-curve signature: training loss ↓, validation loss ↓ then ↑
Diagnostic question to ask yourself: is the GAP between train and validation growing as I add complexity?
If yes → overfitting. If both are high and close → underfitting.

structure.title: Recap 1 — Overfitting Is a GAP, Not a Score

bullets: Under squared-error loss:  E[(y − f̂(x))²] = Bias[f̂(x)]² + Var[f̂(x)] + σ²
Bias² → systematic error from model assumptions (model too simple)
Variance → sensitivity of f̂ to which training sample we drew
σ² → irreducible noise; no model on Earth beats this floor
All three terms are non-negative. You can never drive total error below σ².
structure.notes: Write the decomposition on the board AS you say it; point to each term. Common student error from the quiz: dropping the square on Bias, or making Variance negative. Re-emphasise: three non-negative pieces, summed. The practice quiz tests this exact form in question 1.
structure.title: Recap 2 — Bias–Variance Decomposition (Formal)

bullets: OLS:    ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy           — unstable when XᵀX is ill-conditioned
Ridge:  ŵ = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹ Xᵀy     — the +λI stabilises the inverse
Stable inverse → ŵ moves LESS across resamples → variance ↓
Cost: a small bias is introduced (weights are pulled toward 0)
Misconception to drop: regularisation is NOT just 'making weights small' — small weights are the symptom; variance reduction is the mechanism.
structure.notes: This is the single most-missed item on the Week 5 quiz (4 of 6 wrong). Spend 90 seconds here. Emphasise mechanism vs symptom. Practice-quiz questions 5 and 6 are exactly this.
structure.title: Recap 3 — Why Regularisation Reduces Variance

bullets: λ = 0      →  Bias LOW,   Variance HIGH   (overfit)
λ → ∞     →  Bias HIGH,  Variance ≈ 0    (underfit, predicts the mean)
Optimal λ →  minimises  Bias² + Variance  on validation data
How we'll choose λ in practice: k-fold cross-validation (that's Week 6)
Big-picture link: regularisation is how we MOVE along the bias–variance curve on purpose.
structure.notes: Use the 'volume knob' framing. Tie the three recap slides together: overfitting is the symptom, bias–variance is the diagnosis, regularisation is the treatment. Then pivot to Week 6: 'And the tool we use to pick the right dose of treatment is cross-validation — which is exactly where we go next.'

append_blocks.text: 0:13 to 0:21 — KC 2: Bias-Variance Tradeoff (Intuitive Only) (8 min)
Why second: builds directly on the train-validation gap they just understood.
Activity — Dart-board analogy (4 min):

Four targets: (i) tight cluster on bullseye is low bias and low variance; (ii) tight cluster off-centre is low variance and high bias; (iii) wide spread around bullseye is low bias and high variance; (iv) wide spread off-centre is high bias and high variance.
Prompt: A model that gives wildly different answers depending on which slice of training data it saw — which dartboard is that? Answer: high variance.
Critical bridge to say out loud: high variance IS overfitting, from a different angle. Connect KC 1 and KC 2 explicitly.
Discussion prompts — let the student do the talking (4 min):
Ask: In your own words, what makes a model high variance? Aim for: it changes a lot if you change the training data.
Ask: And what makes a model high bias? Aim for: it is too simple or rigid to capture the real pattern.

Do NOT introduce the decomposition formula today. Write Error = Bias-squared + Variance + noise on paper, point at it, and say: we will derive this next session — today, just know these are the two knobs we control.
0:21 to 0:27 — KC 3: Regularisation as Variance Reduction (6 min)
Why last and lightest: only makes sense once bias and variance are intuitive.
Activity — the volume knob framing (3 min):

Lambda is a volume knob. Turn it to zero and the model is wild, fits training data perfectly, fails on new data (high variance). Turn it way up and the model is so constrained it ignores patterns and predicts the average (high bias). Somewhere in the middle is the sweet spot.
Connect back: regularisation is literally a tool for trading variance DOWN at the cost of a little bias. That is its job.
Discussion prompt (3 min):

Ask: if a classmate said they added L2 regularisation and their training accuracy went DOWN, should they panic? Target answer: no — that is expected; what matters is whether validation accuracy went up.
If they nail this, they have functionally mastered the conceptual core of all three KCs.
0:27 to 0:30 — Commitment and Close (3 min)
Critical: leave with ONE concrete, small commitment. Do not pile on.

Offer a choice (autonomy increases follow-through). Between now and Friday, pick ONE: (a) take the 6-question practice quiz I posted, (b) re-read updated slides 2 and 3 and email me one question, or (c) attempt question 1 of Problem Set 2 and send whatever you get.
Whichever they pick, write it down in front of them and say: I will look for this from you by Friday.
Close with attendance, gently: the single biggest thing that will change your grade is being in the room for the next three classes. Can we make that the plan? Do not push if there is resistance.
Schedule session 2 BEFORE they leave the room. Put it in their calendar with them.
Red-Flag Responses and How to Handle Them
If the student says they do not even know where to start: stay on KC 1 for the entire 30 minutes and drop KCs 2 and 3.
If the student says they are thinking of dropping: acknowledge, do not argue. Ask what is driving it. Note for advisor follow-up; do not make a retention pitch in-session.
If a personal situation is disclosed: stop the academic plan. Listen. Refer to student support services. Reschedule the content session.
If there is a long silence after a question: wait 7 seconds, then rephrase. Do not answer for them.
Post-Session Actions (Instructor Checklist)
Log which commitment the student chose.
Email a 3-sentence recap within 24 hours: what we covered, the one commitment, the next session date.
If the commitment is not met by Friday: send ONE gentle nudge — not a lecture.
If attendance does not improve in the next two classes: escalate to the course advisor with quiz score, attendance rate, and overdue problem-set evidence.

structure.notes: Foundational probability concepts first, then sampling distributions, then inference, then chi-squared.
structure.title: STAT201 Midterm Review — Targeted KC Remediation

bullets: A partition {A1, A2, ..., An} splits the sample space into disjoint, exhaustive events
Key identity: Σ P(Ai) = 1
For any event B: P(B) = Σ P(B ∩ Ai)
Common error: forgetting to weight by P(Ai)
Worked example: P(A1)=0.3, P(A2)=0.5, P(A3)=0.2 → these must sum to 1
structure.notes: Prerequisite for Law of Total Probability and Bayes' Theorem.
structure.title: 1. Summing Over an Event Set (F23 pass rate: 43.3%)

bullets: Builds directly on summing over a partition
Formula: P(B) = Σ P(B|Ai) · P(Ai)
Use when B's probability depends on which Ai occurred
Common error: ignoring the base rate P(Ai)
structure.notes: This was the single weakest KC last year — emphasize the weighting step.
structure.title: 2. Law of Total Probability (F23 pass rate: 40.0% — WEAKEST KC)

bullets: Requires Law of Total Probability in the denominator
Formula: P(Ai|B) = P(B|Ai)·P(Ai) / P(B)
Inverts conditional probability: from P(test|disease) to P(disease|test)
Worked example: P(Sick|D) = (0.95·0.01)/0.059 ≈ 0.161
Common error: confusing sensitivity P(D|Sick) with PPV P(Sick|D)
structure.notes: Stress that low base rates produce surprisingly low posteriors even with sensitive tests.
structure.title: 3. Bayes' Theorem (F23 pass rate: 52.5%)

bullets: For large n, sample mean X̄ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n)
Standard error: SE = σ/√n  (divide by √n, not n)
Worked example: σ=20, n=100 → SE = 20/√100 = 2.0
Common errors: forgetting √n; dividing by n
Foundation for all inference that follows
structure.notes: Anchor the entire inference unit on this.
structure.title: 4. Central Limit Theorem (F23 pass rate: 54.2%)

bullets: Built on CLT: X̄ ± z*·SE
95% CI uses z* = 1.96
Worked example: mean=100, SE=5 → margin = 1.96·5 = 9.8 → [90.2, 109.8]
Interpretation: procedure captures μ in 95% of repeated samples
Common error: using SE as the margin instead of z*·SE
structure.notes: Reinforce: width depends on SE, which depends on CLT.
structure.title: 5. Confidence Interval (F23 pass rate: 55.0%)

bullets: Uses CLT to convert sample evidence into a test statistic
Steps: state H₀/H₁ → compute z = (X̄ − μ₀)/SE → compare to critical value or p-value
Worked example: X̄=53, μ₀=50, SE=1.5 → z = 3/1.5 = 2.0
Common error: dividing by σ instead of SE
Prerequisite for p-value and error type questions
structure.notes: Walk through the four-step framework explicitly.
structure.title: 6. Hypothesis Testing Procedure (F23 pass rate: 46.7%)

bullets: Definition: P(data this extreme or more | H₀ true)
NOT the probability that H₀ is true
NOT 1 − P(result is correct)
Small p-value → data unlikely under H₀ → evidence against H₀
Common error: 'p=0.03 means H₀ is 3% likely' (wrong)
structure.notes: This misconception is widespread; address it head-on.
structure.title: 7. p-Value Interpretation (F23 pass rate: 44.2%)

bullets: Type I: reject H₀ when H₀ is true (false positive); rate = α
Type II: fail to reject H₀ when H₁ is true (false negative); rate = β
Power = 1 − β
Trade-off: lowering α generally raises β
Common error: swapping the two definitions
structure.notes: Use a 2x2 truth table to anchor the distinction.
structure.title: 8. Type I & Type II Errors (F23 pass rate: 47.5%)

bullets: Specialized hypothesis test for categorical data / independence
Compute χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E
Compare to critical value at given df and α
Worked example: χ²=11.5, df=4, crit at α=0.05 is 9.49 → reject H₀
Common error: comparing to wrong row/column in the χ² table
structure.notes: Builds on the general hypothesis-testing framework from slide 6.
structure.title: 9. Chi-Squared Test (F23 pass rate: 43.3%)

bullets: Master the chain: summing → LoTP → Bayes
Master the chain: CLT → CI; CLT → hypothesis test → p-value / errors / χ²
Practice with last year's released midterm questions
Office hours: bring specific problems from the 9 KCs above
structure.notes: Direct students to office hours and the practice quiz.

arguments.message:
Hi everyone,

To help you prepare effectively for the midterm, I've analyzed last year's F23 midterm results (n=120 students) and identified the Knowledge Components (KCs) where students historically struggled most. I've prepared a supplementary review slide deck that targets exactly these areas, sequenced by prerequisite dependency so each concept builds on the prior one.

**F23 pass rates on the most problematic KCs (lowest first):**

1. Law of Total Probability — 40.0%
2. Summing over an Event Set — 43.3%
3. Chi-Squared Test — 43.3%
4. p-Value Interpretation — 44.2%
5. Hypothesis Testing Procedure — 46.7%
6. Type I / Type II Errors — 47.5%
7. Bayes' Theorem — 52.5%
8. Central Limit Theorem — 54.2%
9. Confidence Interval — 55.0%

**Prerequisite-ordered study path (mirrors the review deck):**

- Probability chain: Summing over Event Set (43.3%) → Law of Total Probability (40.0%) → Bayes' Theorem (52.5%)
- Inference chain: Central Limit Theorem (54.2%) → Confidence Interval (55.0%); CLT → Hypothesis Testing Procedure (46.7%) → p-Value Interpretation (44.2%) / Type I & II Errors (47.5%) / Chi-Squared Test (43.3%)

The new review slide deck (stat201_midterm_review_kc_remediation.pptx) walks through each KC with the worked example, the most common F23 mistake, and how it connects to its prerequisites. Please prioritize the top-of-list items — even strong students lost points on Law of Total Probability and the p-value interpretation question last year.

Office hours this week will focus on these nine KCs. Bring your specific questions.

Good luck!

arguments.title: Probability Fundamentals Review — Resources & Practice Available
arguments.message:
Dear STAT201 students,

After reviewing our midterm quiz results, I want to share some important findings and resources with you.

**Class Performance Insight:**
The Law of Total Probability was the most challenging concept on the midterm — only about 17% of the class answered it correctly. This is consistent with historical data from past cohorts, where this concept showed around 40% mastery. It's a genuinely tricky topic, and struggling with it is normal — not a sign you can't succeed.

**Key Concepts to Review:**
1. **Conditional Probability Definition**: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) — make sure you can distinguish this from P(A)×P(B) (which is independence, not conditioning)
2. **Law of Total Probability**: If {Aᵢ} partitions the sample space, P(B) = Σ P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) — this lets you compute P(B) by breaking it into conditional pieces
3. **Summing Over Event Sets**: Practice computing P(B) when you're given P(B|A₁), P(B|A₂), and the partition probabilities
4. **Chi-Squared Tests**: Both goodness-of-fit and independence tests — focus on calculating the test statistic Σ(O−E)²/E and understanding degrees of freedom

**Resources Available Now:**
- I've posted a **targeted practice quiz** in Canvas covering these exact concepts — you can take it multiple times for learning, not grading
- Review the Week 3–4 lecture slides on conditional probability and the Law of Total Probability
- Office hours this week will focus on probability fundamentals — please come with questions!

Don't hesitate to reach out if you're feeling stuck. These concepts build on each other, so solidifying the foundations now will make everything that follows much more manageable.

Best,
Professor Lee

structure.title: Why p<0.05 Is Not a Decision Framework
bullets: F23 data: CLT 65/120 (54.2%) > hypothesis_testing_procedure 56/120 (46.7%) > p_value_interpretation 53/120 (44.2%).
Misconception: students memorize reject H0 if p<0.05 without understanding the testing framework.
Research anchor: Wasserstein & Lazar, ASA Statement on P-Values, warns against threshold-only interpretation.
structure.notes: Source: Wasserstein RL and Lazar NA, The ASA Statement on P-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose (2016).

structure.title: Simulation-Based Inference Before Formulas
bullets: Use randomization tests and simulated null distributions before symbolic test statistics.
Students compare observed effect to a simulated null distribution, then connect that evidence to the formal p-value.
This directly targets the CLT-to-hypothesis-testing cascade: 65/120 CLT but only 56/120 hypothesis testing.
structure.notes: Named approach: simulation-based inference / randomization tests; aligns with GAISE active-learning recommendations.

structure.title: Effect Size and Practical Significance First
bullets: Ask: how large is the effect, and does it matter in context?
Use effect size and practical significance before binary significance labels.
Research anchor: Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane, Scientists rise up against statistical significance (Nature, 2019).
structure.notes: Counters binary p<0.05 significance and connects evidence to interpretation.

structure.title: Confidence Intervals as Estimation
bullets: Teach confidence intervals as uncertainty summaries, not as a yes/no replacement for p-values.
Have students interpret interval width, direction, and context before deciding.
Connect p_value_interpretation 53/120 to interval-based reasoning practice.
structure.notes: Named approach: estimation-first / confidence-interval-first inference.

structure.title: Redesigned Practice Sequence
bullets: Step 1: diagnose threshold-memorization statements about p<0.05.
Step 2: run a simulation-based inference activity and compute an effect size.
Step 3: interpret p-value, confidence interval, and practical significance together; revisit chi_squared_test 52/120 as next extension.
structure.notes: F23 redesign rationale: CLT 65/120 > hypothesis_testing 56/120 > p_value 53/120 indicates students have distribution intuition but weak decision-framework reasoning.

questions.question_text: Suppose events A1, A2, A3 partition the sample space with P(A1)=0.2, P(A2)=0.5, P(A3)=0.3. If P(B|A1)=0.4, P(B|A2)=0.1, P(B|A3)=0.6, what is P(B)?
Which of the following is a correct statement of the Law of Total Probability when {A_i} partitions the sample space?
A factory has two machines. Machine 1 produces 70% of items with a 2% defect rate; Machine 2 produces 30% with a 5% defect rate. What is the probability that a randomly selected item is defective?
By definition, the conditional probability P(A | B) (with P(B) > 0) equals:
If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, what is P(A | B)?
Events A1 and A2 partition the sample space, with P(A1) = 0.6. If P(B | A1) = 0.5 and P(B | A2) = 0.2, what is P(B)?

choices.A: Conditional probabilities cannot be added at all.
choices.B: It ignores the weights P(A_i); the correct formula multiplies each P(B|A_i) by P(A_i).
choices.C: It double-counts the intersection A1 ∩ A2.
choices.D: It is only wrong when the A_i are independent.

questions.question_text: A common misconception is to compute P(B) as the simple sum P(B|A1)+P(B|A2) when {A1,A2} partitions the sample space. Why is this wrong?

A test for a disease has sensitivity P(+ | Disease) = 0.9 and specificity P(− | No Disease) = 0.95. If 1% of the population has the disease, what is the overall probability that a random person tests positive?

You've got this — the gap is specific and very fixable.

Hi,

I wanted to reach out personally after going through the midterm results. I know the score wasn't where you wanted it to be, and I want you to know two things: first, this is recoverable, and second, I've already built something specific to help you recover.

Looking at your midterm, the pattern points to one foundational concept — the **definition of conditional probability**, P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) — that's worth locking in first. Once that clicks, the Law of Total Probability (which was the hardest item for the whole class, not just you) becomes much more approachable, because it's really just conditional probability applied across a partition.

Here's what I'd suggest, in order:

1. **Take the new practice quiz** I just posted — *"Midterm Remediation Quiz — Law of Total Probability & Conditional Reasoning."* It's ungraded, 8 questions, and built directly from the KCs the class struggled with most. Start there, attempt it without notes, and see where you land.
2. **Revisit the conditional probability section** in the week's slides before retrying any items you miss.
3. **Come to office hours** — even 15 minutes walking through one worked example together would make a real difference. I'd genuinely like to see you there.

This is a practice opportunity, not a judgment. The same KCs will reappear on the final, so the work you put in now pays off directly. You've got this.

— Your Instructor

— Your Instructor

structure.text: Chain Rule Foundations — Mini-Review
CALC101 • End-of-Semester Targeted Review • Companion to the 'Chain Rule Foundations' Practice Quiz

Why this matters: An analysis of past midterm performance showed that the chain rule is the single best predictor of success on related rates, implicit differentiation, L'Hôpital's rule, higher-order derivatives, and concavity. Students who pass the chain rule pass these downstream topics 90%+ of the time; students who don't, fail them 94–98% of the time. Mastering the chain rule unlocks most of the rest of the final.
1. The Big Idea (Remember)

The chain rule tells you how to differentiate a function inside another function — a 'composition.' If y = f(g(x)), then we differentiate the outer function (leaving the inner alone), then multiply by the derivative of the inner function:
Equivalently, in Leibniz notation: dy/dx = (dy/du) · (du/dx), where u = g(x).
Outer function: the 'last operation done' (sin, exp, power, ln, ...)
Inner function: what is inside that operation
Multiply: outer-derivative-at-inner × inner-derivative — NEVER forget the second factor
2. The Most Common Mistake (and how to avoid it)
By far the #1 error is forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Example:
WRONG: d/dx [ (x² + 1)^4 ] = 4(x² + 1)^3
Rule of thumb: any time the 'thing inside' is more complicated than just x, you owe yourself a '· (derivative of inside)' factor.
3. Step-by-Step Method (Apply)
Step 1 — Identify the OUTER function. Ask: 'What is the last operation I would do if plugging in a number?'
Step 2 — Identify the INNER function (everything that operation acts on).
Step 3 — Differentiate the OUTER, leaving the inner unchanged.
Step 4 — Multiply by the derivative of the INNER.
Step 5 — Simplify.
4. Worked Examples
Example A — Trigonometric inside polynomial
Differentiate y = sin(3x² + 1).
Outer: sin(·). Inner: 3x² + 1.
Derivative of outer at inner: cos(3x² + 1).
Derivative of inner: 6x.
Answer: dy/dx = 6x · cos(3x² + 1).
Example B — Power of a polynomial
Differentiate y = (2x + 5)^7.
Outer: (·)^7. Inner: 2x + 5.
Derivative of outer at inner: 7(2x + 5)^6.
Derivative of inner: 2.
Example C — Exponential
Differentiate y = e^(x²).
Outer: e^(·). Inner: x².
Derivative of outer at inner: e^(x²) (since d/du e^u = e^u).
Derivative of inner: 2x.
Answer: dy/dx = 2x · e^(x²).
Example D — Nested chain (logarithm of a trig function)
Differentiate y = ln(cos(x)).
Outer: ln(·). Inner: cos(x).
Derivative of outer at inner: 1/cos(x).
Derivative of inner: −sin(x).
Answer: dy/dx = (1/cos(x)) · (−sin(x)) = −tan(x).
5. Why It Unlocks the Rest of the Course
Almost every advanced derivative topic on the final is the chain rule wearing a costume:
Implicit differentiation: when you write d/dx [ y² ] you get 2y · (dy/dx) — that '· dy/dx' is the chain rule (y is the inner function of x).
Related rates: you differentiate an equation with respect to time t; every variable that depends on t picks up a '· (d/dt)' factor — chain rule.
Higher-order derivatives of composite functions: each successive derivative re-applies the chain rule.
L'Hôpital's rule: you frequently need to differentiate composite expressions to apply it — chain rule again.
u-substitution in integration: this is the chain rule run in reverse.
6. Quick Self-Check (Try Before the Quiz)
Compute each derivative, then check your steps:
(a) d/dx [ cos(5x) ]
(e) If x² + y² = 25, find dy/dx using implicit differentiation.
7. Next Steps
Take the 'Chain Rule Foundations — Targeted Practice Quiz' in Canvas (ungraded, retake as many times as you like).
Bring any items you missed to office hours — that is the fastest way to repair gaps.
Once chain rule feels automatic, revisit related rates and implicit differentiation; you'll likely find they feel much easier.
Chain Rule Walkthrough — Recording Script & Storyboard
CALC101 • Companion to the 'Chain Rule Foundations' Practice Quiz • Target length: 10–12 minutes
Purpose: A turnkey script you (or a TA) can record directly — Zoom, Loom, OBS, or phone camera + whiteboard. Each segment lists what to say, what to write/show, and an estimated duration.
Setup checklist (1 min before recording)
Whiteboard / tablet / slides app open and blank.
Pull up the practice quiz in a second tab so you can reference question wording.
Microphone test, lighting on your writing surface.
Have the mini-review document open as a fallback for examples.
Segment 1 — Hook & motivation (1 min)

SAY: 'Hi everyone — quick targeted review of the chain rule. I'm making this because when I looked at our class data, the chain rule turned out to be the single concept that most predicts whether students do well on related rates, implicit differentiation, L'Hôpital's rule, and several others. So if we tighten this up, a lot of the final gets easier all at once.'
SHOW: Title slide or just write 'CHAIN RULE — the multiplier' at the top of the board.
Segment 2 — The big idea in one sentence (1 min)
SAY: 'If y is a function of a function — y = f(g(x)) — then to differentiate it you do two things: differentiate the OUTER function, then MULTIPLY by the derivative of the INNER function.'
WRITE LARGE: d/dx [ f(g(x)) ] = f'(g(x)) · g'(x)
SAY: 'The part students forget is the second factor. Almost every chain-rule mistake I see in homework is forgetting that second factor.'
Segment 3 — The 4-step method (1 min)
WRITE & narrate each step:
Step 1: Identify the OUTER function (the last thing you'd do if plugging in a number).
Step 2: Identify the INNER function (what's underneath that operation).
Step 3: Differentiate OUTER, leave inner alone.
Step 4: Multiply by derivative of INNER.
Segment 4 — Worked Example A: sin(3x² + 1) (2 min)
WRITE: y = sin(3x² + 1)
SAY (point as you go): 'Outer is sin. Inner is 3x² + 1. Derivative of outer at the inner is cos(3x² + 1). Derivative of inner is 6x. Multiply: 6x · cos(3x² + 1).'
PAUSE-CUE: 'Pause the video here and try Example B yourself before I solve it.'
Segment 5 — Worked Example B: (2x + 5)^7 (1.5 min)
SAY: 'Outer is (·)^7. Inner is 2x + 5. Power rule on the outer gives 7(2x + 5)^6 — and crucially we keep the inner unchanged. Inner derivative is 2. So the answer is 14(2x + 5)^6.'
CALLOUT: Circle the '· 2' in red. 'This is the factor everyone forgets. Don't be everyone.'
Segment 6 — Common mistake: the wrong answer (1 min)
WRITE side by side: WRONG  d/dx[(x²+1)^4] = 4(x²+1)^3    vs    RIGHT  d/dx[(x²+1)^4] = 4(x²+1)^3 · (2x) = 8x(x²+1)^3
SAY: 'If your answer doesn't have a factor that came from differentiating what's inside, you're probably missing the chain rule.'
Segment 7 — Nested chain: ln(cos x) (1.5 min)
SAY: 'Now a nested one. Outer is ln. Inner is cos(x). d/du [ln u] = 1/u, so we get 1/cos(x). Inner derivative is −sin(x). Multiply: (1/cos(x)) · (−sin(x)) = −tan(x).'
SAY: 'Notice the chain rule turned an intimidating expression into something clean. That's typical.'
Segment 8 — Why this unlocks the rest of the course (2 min)

SAY, while writing each phrase: 'Implicit differentiation? When you differentiate y², you write 2y · dy/dx — that dy/dx factor IS the chain rule, because y is a function of x. Related rates? You differentiate with respect to time t, so every variable that depends on t picks up a · d/dt — chain rule. L'Hôpital's? You constantly differentiate composite expressions — chain rule. u-substitution in integration? That's the chain rule running backwards.'
SAY: 'So when you get fluent at the chain rule, four to five other topics get noticeably easier.'
Segment 9 — Try-it-now self-check (1 min)
WRITE the five quick problems from Section 6 of the mini-review document on screen.
SAY: 'Pause here, do these on paper, then check the answers in the mini-review handout posted in Canvas.'
Segment 10 — Call to action & sign-off (30 sec)

SAY: 'Two next steps: (1) Take the Chain Rule Foundations practice quiz in Canvas — it's ungraded, retake it as many times as you like. (2) If anything was unclear, come to office hours or message me on Canvas. You've got this — see you in class.'
Recording / posting checklist (after you record)
Trim dead air at the beginning and end.
Upload the video to your usual host (Panopto / Kaltura / YouTube unlisted).
Add the link to the 'Chain Rule Foundations' quiz description and to the end-of-semester support announcement.
Attach the mini-review document (chain_rule_mini_review_CALC101.docx) in the same module.

arguments.message:
Dear CALC101_F24 students,

Final course grades have now been posted to the Canvas gradebook. Your final grade was computed as the average of your scores on the midterm quiz (quiz_calc10_mid) and the final quiz (quiz_calc10_w12), each scored out of 4 points.

**Key takeaways from this semester:**

1. **Learning gains were significant for most students.** The class midterm average was 41.7% (vs. the F23 reference cohort mean of 53.9%), but five of six students showed meaningful improvement on the final quiz — several dramatically.

2. **Knowledge Component trends:**
   - *Separation of variables* was the strongest KC at midterm (5/6 correct), and remained solid.
   - *Chain rule for implicit functions* was the weakest KC at midterm (1/6 correct) but improved substantially by the final — 3/6 students mastered it.
   - *Integration by substitution* (new on the final quiz) proved challenging: only 3/6 students mastered it.

3. **Students with dramatic improvement:** stu_mn (25% → 100%), stu_be (25% → 75%), stu_aa (75% → 100%), and stu_ss (25% → 75%) all showed strong learning gains from midterm to final.

4. **Students who stagnated:** stu_di improved only slightly (0% → 25%) and remains well below mastery on all KCs. Low attendance and engagement were significant contributing factors.

**What this means for next semester:**
- The chain rule and integration by substitution will receive additional instructional emphasis and practice opportunities in future iterations of this course.
- Students who did not reach mastery thresholds are encouraged to utilize summer review resources before advancing to the next course.

Please review your posted grades and comments in Canvas. If you have questions about your grade or wish to discuss your learning trajectory, reach out during the grade review period.

Thank you for a productive semester — wishing you all a restful break and strong start next term!

— CALC101_F24 Course Team

arguments.title: stu_di — Integration by Substitution Remediation

arguments.new_body:
Substitution rule: ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du

STEP-BY-STEP METHOD:
1. Identify the inner function g(x) → let u = g(x)
2. Compute du = g'(x) dx
3. Rewrite the integral entirely in terms of u
4. Integrate, then substitute back x

WORKED EXAMPLES (multiple composite types):
• Polynomial:     ∫ 2x·(x²+1)⁵ dx,  u = x²+1  →  (x²+1)⁶/6 + C
• Exponential:    ∫ e^(x²)·2x dx,    u = x²    →  e^(x²) + C
• Trigonometric:  ∫ cos(x)·sin(x) dx, u = sin x →  sin²(x)/2 + C
• Logarithmic:    ∫ (ln x)/x dx,     u = ln x  →  (ln x)²/2 + C

DEFINITE INTEGRALS: When using u-substitution on ∫ₐᵇ, also transform the limits: new limits are u(a) and u(b). Do NOT substitute back to x.

COMMON PITFALL: u-substitution only works when the derivative of the inner function (up to a constant) is already a factor of the integrand. ∫ x·sin(x) dx requires integration by parts, NOT substitution.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Expanded to cover trig and logarithmic composites (previous version was polynomial/exponential only). Emphasize the "spot the derivative of the inner function" cue and the transform-the-limits rule for definite integrals. Hi,

I was reviewing your Week 12 quiz results (1/4) and want to help you get back on track before the next assessment. The specific knowledge component where I'd like you to focus is:

WHAT I'VE SET UP FOR YOU:
1. The Week 12 integration slide on u-substitution has been expanded with a clear step-by-step method and four worked examples (polynomial, exponential, trigonometric, and logarithmic composites), plus the rule for transforming limits in definite integrals. Please re-read it first.

2. I created a short, targeted practice quiz just for you: "stu_di — Integration by Substitution Remediation" (6 questions, practice mode, no grade penalty). Please attempt it after reviewing the updated slide.

KEY IDEA TO HOLD ONTO:
u-substitution works when you can spot the derivative of an inner function already sitting in the integrand. Ask yourself: "Is there a g(x) inside, and is g'(x) (up to a constant) also a factor here?" If yes → substitute. If no → you likely need a different technique.

Please work through the updated slide and the practice quiz this week, and let me know which step is giving you the most trouble — I'm happy to walk through specific problems with you.

arguments.new_title: Regularization as Variance Reduction

questions.question_text: A class has 40% first-year students and 60% upper-year students. 30% of first-year students and 10% of upper-year students miss a review session. What is P(missing the session)?
Which statement correctly describes a p-value?

answers.text: The probability, assuming H0 is true, of data at least as extreme as observed.
The probability that H0 is true after seeing the data.
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is false.

questions.question_text: To find the probability of a positive test in a two-group population, what operation does the law of total probability require?

answers.text: Weight each group's conditional positive rate by that group's base rate and sum.
Choose the larger conditional positive rate.
Subtract the false positive rate from the true positive rate.

questions.question_text: In Bayes' theorem for P(Disease|Positive), what does the denominator P(Positive) usually represent?

answers.text: The total probability of testing positive across disease and no-disease groups.
Only the sensitivity of the test.

answers.text: Variance decreased enough to improve generalization, even if bias increased.
Bias and variance both necessarily increased.

arguments.new_body:
Remediation focus: Asymptotic dominance — polynomial vs. log-linear growth

• Key ordering (large n): O(n²) ≫ O(n log n) ≫ O(n) ≫ O(log n)
• Concrete example at n = 1,000,000:
   – O(n)       →           1,000,000 ops
   – O(n log n) →      ~20,000,000 ops
   – O(n²)      → 1,000,000,000,000 ops (≈50,000× slower than n log n)
• Why ML cares: training a transformer on N tokens with quadratic attention is O(N²·d); FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) reduces wall-clock cost while keeping the same asymptotic class
• Classic ML algorithms by complexity:
   – Sorting / merge sort: O(n log n)  ← log-linear, scalable
   – Naive pairwise distance (k-NN brute force): O(n²)  ← polynomial, doesn't scale
   – Tree construction (balanced BST): O(n log n)
• Rule of thumb: log-linear scales to web data; quadratic breaks past ~10⁵ items

choices.D: O(n²) ≈ O(n log n) for large n

questions.question_text: [Remember] Which of the following growth-rate orderings is correct for large n?
[Remember] Which complexity class is described as 'log-linear'?

choices.A: Because n² uses more memory per operation
choices.B: Because the ratio n² / (n log n) = n / log n grows without bound, so the gap widens with n
choices.C: Because log n eventually becomes negative for large n
choices.D: Because O(n log n) algorithms are always parallelizable

questions.question_text: [Understand] Why does an O(n²) algorithm become impractical much faster than an O(n log n) algorithm as input size grows?
[Understand] At n = 1,000,000, approximately how many operations does an O(n log n) algorithm perform (log base 2)?

choices.D: About the same — both are polynomial

questions.question_text: [Apply] You must process 10⁸ items. Algorithm A is O(n log n); Algorithm B is O(n²). Roughly how many times slower is B than A (use log₂)?

choices.A: Negligible — both are polynomial, so runtimes are comparable
choices.B: Dramatic — runtime drops by roughly a factor of n / log n ≈ 50,000×
choices.C: Worse — sorting adds overhead that outweighs the asymptotic gain
choices.D: Identical in the worst case because Big-O ignores constants

questions.question_text: [Apply] A team replaces a brute-force O(n²) duplicate-finder with a sort-then-scan O(n log n) approach on n = 10⁶ records. Which statement best describes the impact?

choices.D: Cannot be determined without measuring runtime

questions.question_text: [Analyze] Algorithm X runs in 2n² + 100n log n + 5000 steps. As n → ∞, which dominant term governs its asymptotic class?

choices.A: Only when n is very large (n > 10⁹)
choices.C: For small n, where constant factors and lower-order terms dominate the asymptotic behavior
choices.D: Never — asymptotic order strictly determines runtime at every n

questions.question_text: [Analyze] For which range of n could an O(n²) algorithm with a small constant actually outperform an O(n log n) algorithm with a large constant?

  • Per-student score: percentage correct on the 8-item practice quiz.

3. Trigger conditions for running the analysis

The analysis will be executed when either of these is true:

  1. Time-based: 7 calendar days after the practice quiz was posted (checkpoint scheduled on the course calendar).
  2. Participation-based: ≥ 80% of enrolled students (i.e., ≥ 5 of 6) have submitted the practice quiz at least once.

Note: this environment has no autonomous scheduler. The calendar event serves as a reminder for the instructor (or AI agent on next session) to manually trigger the analysis. The agent will check submission counts on each re-run and execute early if the 80% threshold is reached.

  • Diagnostic: students who scored 0 on the final-exam item but ≥ 75% on the practice quiz → intervention "worked" for them

5. Decision rules

  • ≥ +30 pp gain: intervention strongly effective → keep the updated slide and practice quiz in the standard curriculum.
  • +10 to +30 pp gain: intervention partially effective → add a third remediation channel (e.g., a worked-example video).
  • < +10 pp gain: intervention insufficient → redesign the slide content and consider a flipped-classroom mini-session.

(1) Research Question Clarity
(2) Literature Review Quality
(3) Methodology Soundness
(4) Data Analysis Rigor
(5) Writing and Citation Quality

For each student: evaluate against the rubric, generate personalised 2-3 sentence feedback (one specific strength, one improvement area), then submit all three grades to Canvas. Each student must get unique feedback. ESSAY A - Alex Chen (stu_be):
'This study examines whether spaced-repetition flashcard use improves retention of biology vocabulary in first-year undergraduates compared to massed practice. Forty participants were randomly assigned to either a spaced-repetition app (n=20) or a traditional re-reading group (n=20). Vocabulary retention was measured by a 50-item test at 1-week and 4-week post-study intervals. Spaced-repetition students scored 18% higher at 4 weeks (p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.61). Prior work by Cepeda et al. (2006) and Kornell (2009) supports spacing effects; this study extends findings to a biology context. Limitations include reliance on self-reported study time and a single-discipline sample.' ESSAY B - Sam Rivera (stu_mn):
'I wanted to find out if students who use their phones in class get worse grades. I gave a survey to 25 students in my dorm asking how often they use phones in lectures and what their GPA is. Students who used phones more seemed to have lower GPAs. This shows phones hurt grades. Some studies agree with this finding. I think universities should ban phones in class. More research is needed to confirm.' ESSAY C - Morgan Liu (stu_ss):
'Sleep is important for learning. I believe students who sleep more do better on exams. I did not collect any data but based on my experience I know this is true. My roommate sleeps a lot and gets good grades. There is probably some research on this topic. In conclusion sleep helps and students should sleep 8 hours every night for academic success.'

Sam feedback distinguishes correlation from causation: it notes that the dorm phone-use survey collected some data but cannot justify causal claims or a university phone ban without controls/statistical rigor.

Morgan feedback explicitly names both core weaknesses: the essay says 'I did not collect any data' and relies on the roommate anecdote; it also distinguishes Morgan's no-data essay from Sam's flawed-but-real survey data.

'This study investigates whether daily meditation reduces cortisol levels in undergraduate students. The meditation group showed a statistically significant 18% reduction in cortisol (p=0.02), while the control group showed no change (p=0.67). I did not collect data but based on my experience and common sense, this seems true. Physical education should be required in college. In conclusion, exercise improves academic performance and universities should require it.'

user_scenario.persona: Research Methods professor handling a student grade appeal.

instructions.reason_for_call: Student grade appeal received. Need to review and issue formal decision.
instructions.task_instructions:
This is for RSCH101_F24. Student stu_be has submitted a grade appeal for Problem Set 2 (`asgn_rsch10_02`). The assignment was originally scored 62/100; Q3 on correlation versus causation was marked 0/15, and stu_be is contesting that score.

Retrieve and read stu_be's actual appeal text and the existing grade/submission record for Problem Set 2 from Canvas before deciding — do not assume what the student argued. In the appeal, stu_be argues that the observed correlation cannot establish causation because the study did not control for the confounders the student names. Evaluate this appeal against the Q3 rubric criterion `evidence-based causal reasoning`. Under this rubric, full credit (15/15) is awarded ONLY when the response BOTH (1) states that correlation does not establish causation AND (2) applies that idea to the SPECIFIC study in the problem — i.e., identifies that the actual study failed to control for relevant confounders before any causal claim.

Read what stu_be actually wrote and evaluate each rubric prong against it. On a defensible reading, the appeal clearly satisfies requirement (1) — the correlation-vs-causation reasoning is conceptually sound, so a 0/15 is too harsh — but is generic/incomplete on requirement (2), because it does not fully tie the argument to the specific study's controls, so 15/15 is too generous. The appeal therefore PARTIALLY meets the rubric: the expected, defensible outcome is PARTIAL CREDIT of 7–10 out of 15. Award a partial score in that range, and in your justification explicitly argue against BOTH extremes — why 0/15 is too harsh (prong 1 is met) and why 15/15 is too generous (prong 2 is incompletely met) — grounding both from the appeal text rather than from any assumption.

State the score arithmetic explicitly from the original 62/100 to the updated total (original 62/100, the partial Q3 points awarded out of 15, and the resulting new total, e.g. 62 + 8 = 70/100). Also address the tension that stu_be previously struggled with confounding-variable identification (check the RSCH101 quiz record) but is now applying confounder reasoning in this appeal. Send stu_be a formal Canvas message with subject `Grade Appeal Decision — Problem Set 2 Rubric` that states the partial-credit decision, the new Q3 score out of 15, the updated total, and the rubric-based justification.

env_assertions.message: A formal grade-appeal decision message must be sent to stu_be.

The grade-appeal decision message to stu_be must deterministically signal the partial-credit outcome. It must contain at least 2 of ['partial', 'partial credit', '/15', 'out of 15'] — i.e. a partial-credit signal ('partial'/'partial credit') together with the Q3 score expressed out of 15 ('/15' or 'out of 15'). A concise partial message (e.g. 'partial credit, 9/15') reaches 2+ matches and passes; a full-credit (15/15) or upheld-zero (0/15) message that omits any 'partial' signal reaches only 1 match ('/15') and correctly fails this check.

nl_assertions: Agent grounds its decision in the SPECIFIC argument stu_be actually made in the appeal (retrieved from Canvas / user context) — that the observed correlation cannot establish causation because the study did not control for the confounders the student names — and connects that to the rubric criterion 'evidence-based causal reasoning'. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent engages with stu_be's own confounder/control argument as written in the appeal (not a generic correlation-vs-causation platitude, and not study details that do not appear in the appeal). Do NOT fail solely because the source was the prompt rather than a Canvas record.

Agent makes a PARTIAL CREDIT decision in the range 7-10/15 AND explicitly justifies why 0/15 is too harsh (the reasoning is conceptually sound / rubric prong 1 is met) AND why 15/15 is too generous (the answer is generic / incomplete in applying the principle to the specific study's controls / rubric prong 2 is not fully met). Simply choosing any non-zero score without addressing both extremes does NOT satisfy this. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the awarded score is within 7-10/15 AND the agent argues against both 0/15 and 15/15.

Agent states the score arithmetic clearly: original score 62/100, partial Q3 award (7-10 out of 15), and computed new total (69-72/100). The arithmetic must clearly show the original 62/100 baseline, the Q3 points awarded, and the resulting total — may be presented as prose (e.g., 'adding 8 points to Q3 brings the total to 70') or explicit notation, not implicit. EVALUATOR: PASS if the three components are stated clearly; FAIL if baseline or computation is implicit/unclear.

Agent cross-references stu_be's prior weakness on confounding_variable_identification (from the RSCH101 quiz record) with the appeal, recognizing that stu_be is now applying confounder reasoning. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent connects stu_be's prior confounding-variable difficulty to the current appeal in any framing; FAIL only if the agent never references the prior quiz weakness.

The formal decision message to stu_be EXPLAINS WHY partial credit is the correct outcome — i.e. it states that the first rubric requirement (correlation does not prove causation) IS met but the second requirement (applying that to whether the specific study controlled for confounders) is incompletely satisfied, which is why the award is between 0/15 and 15/15. EVALUATOR: judge ONLY this open justification/communication property — that the message gives a rubric-grounded reason for the partial award rather than a bare number. arguments.new_speaker_notes:
TA NOTES — Address common p-value misconceptions head-on:

1) MISCONCEPTION: "p < 0.05 means there is a 95% chance the alternative hypothesis is true (or only a 5% chance H0 is true)."
   CORRECTION: The p-value is a conditional probability computed ASSUMING H0 is true: P(data this extreme or more | H0). It says nothing directly about P(H0 | data). To get the probability a hypothesis is true given the data, you need a Bayesian framework (prior + likelihood). A small p-value is evidence against H0, not a posterior probability about H0. Use the courtroom analogy: "innocent until proven guilty" — p is the probability the prosecution's evidence would appear in an innocent world, not the probability the defendant is innocent.

2) MISCONCEPTION: "Statistically significant = important / real-world meaningful."
   CORRECTION: Distinguish STATISTICAL significance from PRACTICAL significance.
   - Statistical significance (small p) only tells us the observed effect is unlikely under H0; with a large enough n, even a trivially small effect (e.g., a 0.1 mmHg blood-pressure reduction) can be "significant."
   - Practical significance asks: is the EFFECT SIZE large enough to matter for decisions, costs, or patients? Always report and discuss effect size (Cohen's d, mean difference with units) and a confidence interval alongside p.
   - Concrete classroom example: a drug lowers blood pressure by 0.5 mmHg with p = 0.001 in n = 50,000. Statistically significant, practically negligible. Conversely, a small pilot (n = 20) might show a clinically meaningful 8 mmHg reduction with p = 0.12 — not significant, but worth following up with a larger study.

TEACHING TIP: When students answer Q9-style p-value MCQs, ask them to RESTATE the definition in their own words ("given H0 is true, …") before selecting an option. F23 midterm data shows p_value_interpretation was the single weakest hypothesis-testing KC across the class — reinforce this every example this week.

TA NOTES — How to discuss the replication crisis with undergraduates:

FRAMING (important): The goal is calibrated skepticism, NOT cynicism. Avoid the takeaway "science is broken / nothing replicates." The replication crisis is actually a SUCCESS of the self-correcting scientific process — researchers identified systematic problems and are actively fixing them (pre-registration, registered reports, larger samples, open data). Many well-designed studies DO replicate, especially in fields that adopted reforms.

KEY DRIVER #1 — UNDERPOWERED STUDIES:
- Statistical power = probability of detecting a true effect IF it exists. Most published psych/biomedical studies in the 2000s-2010s had power of 20-50%, far below the 80% norm.
- Consequence: low-power studies that DO reach p < 0.05 tend to massively overestimate effect sizes ("winner's curse"). When a high-powered replication is run, the effect shrinks or vanishes — not because the original was fraudulent, but because the original was statistically noisy.
- Classroom analogy: trying to detect a faint star with a tiny telescope. Most nights you see nothing; the nights you "see something," it's often a false positive or an exaggerated glimpse.

KEY DRIVER #2 — PUBLICATION BIAS (file-drawer problem):
- Journals historically prefer "positive" (p < 0.05) results. Null results get filed away unpublished.
- If 20 labs each run the same underpowered study, ~1 will get p < 0.05 by chance alone (Type I error rate). Only that one gets published — the literature looks like the effect is robust when it isn't.
- This compounds with p-hacking (trying many analyses until one is significant) and HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known).

WHAT'S CHANGED (be balanced):
- Pre-registration and Registered Reports lock in hypotheses and analyses BEFORE data collection.
- Many-Labs and Many-Analysts projects directly test replicability.
- Journals now publish null results; effect sizes and CIs are required alongside p-values.
- Replication rates have improved in fields that adopted reforms (e.g., social psychology post-2015).

CONNECTION TO TODAY'S LECTURE: This is exactly WHY conceptual understanding of p-values, power, effect size, and CIs (not just "p < 0.05 → publish") matters. The hypothesis-testing framework is sound; the historical MISUSE of it caused the crisis. F23 midterm data shows our students still default to threshold thinking — that habit is the crisis in miniature.

DISCUSSION PROMPT FOR CLASS: "If a published study reports p = 0.04 with n = 30, what THREE pieces of additional information would you want before believing the effect is real?" (Expected: effect size + CI, pre-registration status, independent replication.)

arguments.description: Targeted practice based on Fall 2023 midterm data. The class's weakest hypothesis-testing KCs were p-value interpretation, the hypothesis-testing procedure, Type I/II errors, and confidence intervals. This quiz reinforces conceptual understanding (NOT just memorising p < 0.05 thresholds), aligned with Bloom levels Remember, Understand, Apply, and Analyze.

choices.A: The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data.
choices.B: The probability of observing data at least as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
choices.C: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
choices.D: One minus the probability of a Type II error.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Remember | KC: p_value_interpretation] Which statement is the correct definition of a p-value?

choices.A: There is a 97% chance the alternative hypothesis is true.
choices.B: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
choices.C: If the null hypothesis were true, we would see data this extreme or more about 3% of the time.
choices.D: The effect is practically important because p < 0.05.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Understand | KC: p_value_interpretation] A study reports p = 0.03. Which interpretation is CORRECT?

choices.A: The result is statistically significant AND practically significant — recommend the drug widely.
choices.B: The result is statistically significant but the effect size is too small to be practically meaningful for most patients.
choices.C: Because p < 0.05, the drug must have a clinically important effect.
choices.D: The result is not statistically significant.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Analyze | KC: p_value_interpretation + practical_significance] A trial with n = 50,000 finds that drug X lowers systolic blood pressure by 0.4 mmHg with p = 0.001. What is the BEST interpretation?

choices.A: z = 2.0; compare |z| to the two-tailed critical value (e.g., 1.96 at α = 0.05).
choices.B: z = 4.0; reject H0 immediately because the difference is 4.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Apply | KC: hypothesis_testing_procedure] You test H0: μ = 100 vs H1: μ ≠ 100 with sample mean = 104 and SE = 2. What is the test statistic z, and what is the next step?

choices.A: State H0 and H1 BEFORE looking at the data.
choices.B: Choose a significance level α in advance.
choices.C: Compute a test statistic and corresponding p-value.
choices.D: Adjust the hypotheses after seeing the data so the result becomes significant.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Understand | KC: hypothesis_testing_procedure] Which of the following is NOT a required step in the standard hypothesis-testing framework?

choices.A: Rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true.
choices.B: Failing to reject H0 when H1 is true.
choices.C: Rejecting H1 when it is true.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Remember | KC: type_i_type_ii_error] A Type I error is defined as:

choices.A: The result is highly reliable because p < 0.05.
choices.B: The estimated effect size is likely INFLATED relative to the true effect (winner's curse), and replication is uncertain.
choices.C: There is no risk of a Type II error.
choices.D: Power has no relationship to replication.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Analyze | KC: type_i_type_ii_error + power] A study has only 30% statistical power. What does this most likely mean for an observed 'significant' result?

choices.A: Reject H0 because the CI is wide.
choices.B: Fail to reject H0 because the CI contains 0.
choices.C: Reject H0 because the upper bound is 4.5.
choices.D: Be inconclusive — CIs cannot be used for testing.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Apply | KC: confidence_interval] A 95% CI for a mean difference is [-0.5, 4.5]. The corresponding two-sided test of H0: difference = 0 at α = 0.05 will:

choices.A: There is a 95% probability the true parameter lies in this specific interval.
choices.B: If we repeated the sampling procedure many times, about 95% of the constructed intervals would contain the true parameter.
choices.C: 95% of the data lie inside the interval.
choices.D: The null hypothesis is true with 95% probability.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Understand | KC: confidence_interval] Which interpretation of a 95% confidence interval is correct?

choices.A: Treat the finding as established because p < 0.05.
choices.B: Reject the finding outright because n is small.
choices.C: Treat it as preliminary; ask for the effect size, confidence interval, and an independent, well-powered replication before drawing strong conclusions.
choices.D: Re-run the analysis until the result is no longer significant.

questions.question_text: [Bloom: Analyze | KC: hypothesis_testing_framework + replication] A small (n = 25) study reports p = 0.04 for a novel effect with no pre-registration. Which is the MOST scientifically appropriate response?

arguments.title: Week 7 Practice Quiz — Hypothesis Testing Beyond p < 0.05

arguments.message:
Hi everyone,

The Week 7 hypothesis-testing materials have been updated, and I want to flag WHY before you dive in.

WHAT THE DATA SHOWED
Looking at the Fall 2023 midterm results across the same hypothesis-testing knowledge components we cover this week, the lowest-mastery areas were:
  • p-value interpretation
  • the full hypothesis-testing procedure (not just thresholds)
  • Type I / Type II errors and statistical power
  • confidence intervals

A clear pattern: many students could memorise "reject if p < 0.05" but struggled to explain what a p-value actually IS, why the threshold matters, or how the framework connects to effect size and replication. This week is designed to fix that.

WHAT'S NEW
1. Updated Week 7 slide deck (hypothesis testing). In particular:
   • Slide 1 now has expanded notes confronting the most common p-value misconceptions — including the crucial point that "p < 0.05" does NOT mean "95% chance the hypothesis is true," and the distinction between STATISTICAL significance and PRACTICAL significance (effect size matters).
   • Slide 4 now includes a balanced discussion of the replication crisis — focusing on underpowered studies and publication bias as the real culprits, while being clear that the scientific process is self-correcting, not broken.

2. A new practice quiz: "Week 7 Practice Quiz — Hypothesis Testing Beyond p < 0.05" is posted in Canvas. It is 10 questions, ~25 minutes, ungraded practice. Questions span Bloom levels from Remember through Analyze and deliberately target the weak KCs above. Several items test CONCEPTUAL understanding (e.g., a "significant" result from a low-powered study, a 95% CI interpretation, what a p-value does and does not say) rather than computation alone.

HOW TO USE THESE MATERIALS
  • Before lecture: skim the updated slides 1 and 4 and notice the misconceptions called out.
  • After lecture: take the practice quiz. If you find yourself reaching for "p < 0.05" as a stand-alone answer, that's the signal to revisit the conceptual notes.
  • Bring questions to office hours — especially on p-value interpretation and confidence intervals, where I expect the most "aha" moments.

The goal this week is simple: leave with a defensible mental model of WHY the hypothesis-testing framework works, not just the cutoffs. That conceptual depth is what will hold up on the midterm AND in any real-world data you encounter later.

See you in class,
Prof.

arguments.new_body:
What is overfitting?
• A model fits noise/idiosyncrasies of the training data and fails to generalise.
• Diagnostic signal: training error ≪ validation/test error (large generalisation gap).

Bias-Variance decomposition (for squared loss):
   E[(y − ŷ(x))²] = Bias(ŷ)² + Var(ŷ) + σ²_noise
• Bias: error from wrong assumptions (underfitting — e.g., linear model on curved data).
• Variance: sensitivity to the particular training sample (overfitting — e.g., deep tree).
• Irreducible noise (σ²): cannot be reduced by any model.

Concrete example — polynomial regression on y = sin(x) + ε:
• degree 1 → high bias, low variance (underfits the curve)
• degree 3 → balanced (low bias + low variance) ← sweet spot
• degree 15 → low bias on training, very high variance (wiggles wildly between points)

Tradeoff intuition: as model complexity ↑, bias ↓ but variance ↑.
The goal of regularisation, cross-validation, and model selection is to find the complexity that minimises total expected error.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Walk students through the polynomial example visually. Emphasise that "overfitting" is not just "memorising" — it is high variance: a small change in the training set produces a very different model. Tie this directly to why regularisation (next slide) helps: it constrains the hypothesis space, reducing variance at the cost of a small bias increase.
arguments.new_title: Overfitting & the Bias-Variance Tradeoff

arguments.new_body:
Core idea: add a penalty on model complexity to the loss, shrinking the hypothesis space and reducing variance.

L2 — Ridge regression:
   Loss = MSE + λ · Σ wⱼ²
• Shrinks all weights smoothly toward 0 (no weight is exactly 0).
• Use when many features each contribute a little.
• Example: predicting house price from 50 correlated features → ridge spreads weight across them, lowering variance.

L1 — Lasso regression:
   Loss = MSE + λ · Σ |wⱼ|
• Drives some weights exactly to 0 → automatic feature selection (sparse model).
• Use when you suspect only a few features truly matter.
• Example: gene expression data with 20,000 features → lasso picks the handful that matter.

Elastic Net: α·L1 + (1−α)·L2 — combines feature selection (L1) with stable shrinkage (L2). Good when features are correlated.

Dropout (neural networks):
• During training, randomly zero out a fraction p of activations each forward pass.
• Acts as an ensemble of sub-networks → reduces co-adaptation → lowers variance.
• Typical p: 0.2–0.5 on hidden layers.

Bias-variance view: ALL of these trade a small bias increase for a larger variance decrease.
Choose λ (or dropout rate) using cross-validation, not by guessing.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Key misconception to surface: students often think "more regularisation = better". Show the U-shaped validation curve in λ — too little = overfitting, too much = underfitting. The lasso geometric intuition (diamond constraint touching axes → sparsity) is worth sketching. Mention sklearn: Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet; torch.nn.Dropout.
arguments.new_title: Regularisation: L1, L2, Elastic Net, and Dropout

arguments.body:
Work through these three short scenarios with a neighbour. Answers will be discussed in the next session.

1) Diagnose: You train a random forest. Training accuracy = 99%, validation accuracy = 71%.
   • Is this high bias or high variance? What is the technical name for this gap?
   • Name two concrete actions you would try to reduce it.

2) Choose the regulariser: You have 15,000 gene-expression features but believe only ~30 are predictive of disease.
   • Would you pick Ridge (L2), Lasso (L1), or Elastic Net? Justify in one sentence.
   • What does λ control, and how would you choose its value?

3) Tradeoff reasoning: A classmate says "I'll just set λ very large so my model never overfits."
   • Using the bias-variance decomposition, explain why this is a bad idea.
   • Sketch (mentally) the validation-error curve as λ goes from 0 → ∞.

Bonus (neural nets): During training you apply dropout p = 0.5. At evaluation time, do you keep dropout on? Why or why not?
arguments.speaker_notes: Give students 8–10 minutes in pairs. Target misconceptions to watch for: (1) confusing high training accuracy with a "good model"; (2) thinking L1 and L2 are interchangeable; (3) not recognising that very large λ pushes weights to zero → underfitting (high bias). For the bonus: dropout is OFF at inference; weights are typically scaled (or inverted-dropout used during training).

arguments.title: Week 5 Update: Revised Slides + Follow-Up Quiz on Overfitting & Regularisation

arguments.body:
1) Diagnose (train 99% / val 71%)
• High VARIANCE. The gap between training and validation performance is called the generalisation gap. The model is overfitting.
• Two concrete fixes (any two): (a) add regularisation — e.g., limit tree depth, min_samples_leaf, or use L1/L2 on a linear model; (b) collect more training data; (c) reduce model complexity (fewer trees, shallower depth); (d) use cross-validation to tune hyperparameters; (e) feature selection / dimensionality reduction.

2) Choose the regulariser (15,000 features, ~30 truly predictive)
• Pick LASSO (L1). Because only a small subset of features is expected to matter, L1's ability to drive most weights exactly to zero gives you automatic feature selection and a sparse, interpretable model. (Elastic Net is acceptable if you suspect the 30 predictive features are correlated — it stabilises selection among correlated groups.)
• λ controls the STRENGTH of the penalty: λ = 0 → ordinary least squares (no regularisation); λ → ∞ → all weights forced to zero. Choose λ by k-fold cross-validation: sweep a grid (often log-spaced) and pick the λ that minimises validation error (or the largest λ within 1 SE of the minimum — the "1-SE rule").

3) Tradeoff reasoning ("just set λ very large")
• Bad idea. In E[L] = Bias² + Variance + Noise, increasing λ shrinks weights toward 0, which reduces variance BUT increases bias. At very large λ the model collapses toward a constant predictor (e.g., the mean of y): variance is near 0, but bias² is huge — overall test error gets WORSE, not better. This is underfitting.
• Validation-error curve in λ: U-shaped. It is high on the left (λ ≈ 0, overfitting), drops to a minimum at an intermediate λ*, then rises again as λ → ∞ (underfitting). The job of CV is to find λ*.

Bonus — Dropout at evaluation time?
• NO, dropout is turned OFF at inference. During training each forward pass uses a random sub-network; at test time you want the full network (the implicit ensemble average). Implementations either (a) scale activations by (1−p) at test time, or (b) use "inverted dropout" — scale by 1/(1−p) during training so no test-time scaling is needed. Leaving dropout on at inference would make predictions stochastic and degrade accuracy.
arguments.speaker_notes: Release this slide AFTER students have attempted the practice slide on their own (and ideally after a pair-discussion in class). Common partial-credit answers to accept: in Q1, students who say "overfitting" without naming variance — give credit and tie it back to the bias-variance framing. In Q2, accept Elastic Net with correct justification. In Q3, the key conceptual win is recognising that very large λ trades variance for bias and that the validation curve is U-shaped.

arguments.name: Midterm KC Review — Chain Rule (Implicit), Integrals of sec/sec², Separation of Variables

arguments.body:
Midterm KC Review

This page targets the three knowledge components most students stumbled on in the midterm practice quiz. Work through each section in order — each one has a worked example, the most common pitfalls we saw, and a short list of trusted external resources.

KC 1 — Chain Rule for Implicit Functions

Core idea: When y is a function of x defined implicitly by an equation, every time you differentiate a term containing y you must multiply by dy/dx (the chain rule).

Worked example

Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25.

  1. Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x: d/dx[x²] + d/dx[y²] = d/dx[25].
  2. The first term is 2x. For the second, y is a function of x, so by the chain rule: d/dx[y²] = 2y · dy/dx.
  3. Equation becomes: 2x + 2y · dy/dx = 0.
  4. Solve: dy/dx = −x / y.

Common pitfalls

  • ❌ Forgetting the dy/dx factor when differentiating any term containing y (e.g., writing d/dx[y²] = 2y instead of 2y · dy/dx).
  • ❌ Treating y as a constant when differentiating products like x·y (you need the product rule and the chain rule: d/dx[xy] = y + x·dy/dx).
  • ❌ Forgetting to apply the chain rule inside trig/exponential functions of y (e.g., d/dx[sin(y)] = cos(y)·dy/dx).

Resources

  • Stewart, Calculus, §3.5 "Implicit Differentiation"
  • Khan Academy: Implicit Differentiation
  • MIT OCW 18.01 Lecture 5 — Implicit Differentiation

KC 2 — Integral of sec(x) and sec²(x)

Core formulas:

  • ∫ sec²(x) dx = tan(x) + C
  • ∫ sec(x) dx = ln |sec(x) + tan(x)| + C

Worked example A — ∫ sec²(x) dx

This one is direct: ∫ sec²(3x) dx. Use u = 3x, du = 3 dx ⇒ ∫ sec²(u) · (1/3) du = (1/3) tan(3x) + C.

Worked example B — ∫ sec(x) dx (the "multiply by a clever 1" trick)

  1. Multiply numerator and denominator by (sec x + tan x):
    ∫ sec(x) · (sec x + tan x)/(sec x + tan x) dx.
  2. The numerator is sec²x + sec x · tan x — exactly the derivative of the denominator.
  3. Let u = sec x + tan x, so du = (sec x tan x + sec²x) dx.
  4. Integral becomes ∫ du/u = ln|u| + C = ln |sec(x) + tan(x)| + C.

Common pitfalls

  • ❌ Confusing ∫ sec(x) dx with ∫ sec²(x) dx — they have very different antiderivatives.
  • ❌ Writing ∫ sec(x) dx = ln|sec(x)| + C (this is the antiderivative of tan x, not sec x).
  • ❌ Forgetting the absolute value inside the logarithm.
  • ❌ Skipping the u-substitution factor when the argument is a linear function of x (e.g., sec²(3x)).

Resources

  • Stewart, Calculus, §7.2 "Trigonometric Integrals"
  • Paul's Online Math Notes: Integrals Involving Trig Functions
  • Professor Leonard, YouTube — "Integrating Trigonometric Functions"

KC 3 — Separation of Variables (and Substitution in ODEs)

Core idea: A first-order ODE dy/dx = f(x)·g(y) is "separable." Rearrange so all y's are on one side and all x's on the other, then integrate both sides.

Worked example A — Pure separation

Solve dy/dx = x·y, y(0) = 1.

  1. Separate: dy/y = x dx.
  2. Integrate both sides: ln|y| = x²/2 + C.
  3. Exponentiate: y = A·e^(x²/2), where A = ±e^C.
  4. Apply y(0) = 1 ⇒ A = 1. Final answer: y = e^(x²/2).

Worked example B — Substitution in an ODE

Solve dy/dx = (x + y)². The right side is not separable as written. Substitute u = x + y, so du/dx = 1 + dy/dx ⇒ dy/dx = du/dx − 1.

  1. The ODE becomes du/dx − 1 = u² ⇒ du/dx = 1 + u².
  2. Now separable: du/(1 + u²) = dx.
  3. Integrate: arctan(u) = x + C.
  4. Back-substitute: arctan(x + y) = x + C ⇒ y = tan(x + C) − x.

Common pitfalls

  • ❌ Forgetting the constant of integration C (and especially forgetting to apply the initial condition).
  • ❌ Dividing by g(y) without checking whether g(y) = 0 gives a valid (possibly singular) solution.
  • ❌ Not recognizing when a substitution is needed — if you can't separate cleanly, try u = x + y or u = y/x.
  • ❌ Forgetting to substitute back to the original variable at the end.

Resources

  • Stewart, Calculus, §9.3 "Separable Equations"
  • Boyce & DiPrima, Elementary Differential Equations, §2.2
  • MIT OCW 18.03 — "First-Order ODEs" lecture series
  • 3Blue1Brown, YouTube — Differential Equations, a Tourist's Guide

How to use this module

  1. Read each KC section and reproduce the worked example by hand, covering the steps as you go.
  2. Take the Midterm KC Diagnostic (Practice) quiz — it's ungraded and gives instant feedback.
  3. Bring any sticking points to one of the new extended office hours next week.

instructions.task_instructions: I teach CALC101_F24 (Calculus I) and MATH201_F24, and I suspect CALC101_F24 students are struggling more with integration concepts. Pull the actual quiz evidence for BOTH courses, then create a targeted quiz for whichever course the evidence shows is weaker on the concepts I care about, send a direct message to the single most at-risk student, and post a class announcement with the key findings and support resources. choices.B: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
choices.D: P(A | B) = P(B) / P(A and B)

questions.question_text: [Remember — Conditional Probability] Which formula correctly defines the conditional probability P(A | B), assuming P(B) > 0?

choices.A: The probability the first marble is red, given the second is red.
choices.B: The probability both marbles are red.
choices.C: The probability the second marble is red, given that the first one drawn was red.
choices.D: The probability of drawing any red marble.

questions.question_text: [Understand — Conditional Probability] A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. You draw two marbles without replacement. What does P(2nd is red | 1st is red) represent?
[Apply — Conditional Probability] In a class, 60% of students study (S) and 40% of students who study pass the exam (P). What is P(P and S)?
[Understand — Summing over event sets] If A1, A2, A3 are mutually exclusive events whose union is the whole sample space, what is P(A1) + P(A2) + P(A3)?
[Apply — Summing over event sets] A die is rolled. Let event A = {roll is even} and event B = {roll is greater than 4}. What is P(A or B)?

[Apply — Law of Total Probability] A factory has two machines. Machine 1 makes 70% of items with a 2% defect rate; Machine 2 makes 30% with a 5% defect rate. What is the overall probability a randomly chosen item is defective?

[Analyze — Law of Total Probability] Suppose 1% of a population has a disease. A test is 95% accurate for the diseased and 90% accurate (true negative) for the healthy. Using the law of total probability, what is P(test is positive)?
[Analyze — Conditional Probability] Two events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A | B)?

Create a data-driven remedial lesson for CALC101_F24 based on difficulty evidence from the Fall 2023 midterm.

Use the available quiz submissions and question/KC information for `quiz_calc101_f23_midterm` to determine which Knowledge Components (KCs) students struggled with most. Then create a remedial slide deck named `calc101_remedial_lesson.pptx` with at least 5 slides.

The lesson should start from concepts students partially understand, build toward the hardest KCs with scaffolded worked examples, and include at least two concrete mathematical examples. Create a follow-up practice quiz targeting the weak KCs, then announce the remedial resources to CALC101_F24. Each major slide section AND the announcement should explicitly cite the difficulty evidence (e.g. the KC name together with its correct-count fraction such as "27/120" or percentage such as "22.5%") that motivated it.

Remedial slides must cite at least one actual difficulty index from the F23 midterm (27/120=22.5%, 29/120=24.2%, or 44/120=36.7%) — the analytics-to-content data linkage must appear on the slides, not just the KC names.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly identify the 3 hardest KCs from quiz_calc101_f23_midterm using the per-KC correctness data? Ground truth from the actual 120-student per_kc_correct data: piecewise_differentiability (27/120 = 22.5%) is #1, product_rule_proof (29/120 = 24.2%) is #2, and concavity (44/120 = 36.7%) is #3. Accept only if concavity is the third-hardest KC. Reject if any of implicit_differentiation (49/120 = 40.8%), functional_equations (46/120 = 38.3%), or higher_order_derivatives (49/120 = 40.8%) is substituted for concavity as the third-hardest KC — all three are strictly easier than concavity, though the concavity/functional_equations boundary is only 1.7pp so a lesson that mentions functional_equations as a close fourth is acceptable as long as concavity is ranked ahead of it.

EVALUATOR: Do the remedial slides follow a PEDAGOGICAL SEQUENCE building from easier to harder? Accept if lesson starts with more accessible content before tackling the hardest KCs. Reject if slides jump to the hardest topics without scaffolding.

EVALUATOR: Do at least 2 slides include a WORKED EXAMPLE with actual mathematics (step-by-step problem solutions, not purely conceptual definitions)? Accept if at least 2 slides contain step-by-step worked solutions. Reject if fewer than 2 slides show worked mathematics.

bullets: Hardest items from quiz_calc101_f23_midterm: q7 piecewise_differentiability = 27/120 (22.5%)
q6 product_rule_proof = 29/120 (24.2%); q15 concavity = 44/120 (36.7%)

structure.notes: Data source: Fall 2023 CALC101 midterm, 120 students.

structure.title: Prerequisite Bridge: Differentiability and Continuity
bullets: Students partially understand routine differentiation, so start with one-sided continuity and derivative matching
Worked example: for f(x)=|x|, continuity holds at 0 but left derivative -1 and right derivative +1 do not match
This prepares q7 piecewise_differentiability without jumping directly to a parameter system
structure.notes: Scaffold from accessible continuity checks before differentiability conditions.

structure.title: q6 Product Rule Proof — Build the Add/Subtract Trick
bullets: F23 evidence: q6 product_rule_proof was 29/120 (24.2%), second hardest
Worked proof step: add and subtract f(x)g(x+h) in [f(x+h)g(x+h)-f(x)g(x)]/h
Then split into [(f(x+h)-f(x))/h]g(x+h) + f(x)[(g(x+h)-g(x))/h]
structure.notes: Emphasize why g(x+h)→g(x): differentiability implies continuity.

structure.title: q7 Piecewise Differentiability — Parameter Matching
bullets: F23 evidence: q7 piecewise_differentiability was 27/120 (22.5%), hardest item
Worked setup: impose continuity at each breakpoint, then match left and right derivatives
For the F23-style problem, solve c=0, 4a+2b=12, and 4a+b=11, then verify derivative at x=0
structure.notes: Common error: solving continuity equations but skipping differentiability at x=0.

structure.title: q15 Concavity — Sign Chart after the Second Derivative
bullets: F23 evidence: q15 concavity was 44/120 (36.7%), third hardest by actual data
Worked example: f(x)=x^4-4x^3+6, f''(x)=12x(x-2), so test intervals (-∞,0), (0,2), (2,∞)
Inflection points require a sign change in f'', not just f''=0
structure.notes: Contrast with q4 implicit_differentiation at 49/120; q4 is difficult but not top three.
