arguments.title: Extra Practice — Integration by Substitution (u-Substitution)

arguments.new_body:
Core rule: ∫ f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du, where u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx

STEP-BY-STEP RECIPE (research-backed: explicit worked-example scaffolding reduces error rate on u-sub problems — Sweller, cognitive load theory):
1. Identify the "inner" function g(x) whose derivative also appears (up to a constant)
2. Let u = g(x); compute du = g'(x) dx
3. Rewrite the integral entirely in u (no x's left!)
4. Integrate in u
5. Back-substitute u = g(x)
6. For DEFINITE integrals: change the bounds using u = g(x) — do NOT back-substitute

WORKED EXAMPLES (covering the three patterns students miss most):
• Polynomial composite: ∫ 2x(x²+1)^5 dx → u = x²+1, du = 2x dx → ∫ u^5 du = (x²+1)^6 / 6 + C
• Exponential composite: ∫ x·e^(x²) dx → u = x², du = 2x dx → (1/2)∫ e^u du = (1/2) e^(x²) + C
• Trig composite (linear inner): ∫ sin(3x) dx → u = 3x, du = 3 dx → (1/3)∫ sin(u) du = -(1/3)cos(3x) + C
• Definite integral: ∫₀¹ 2x(x²+1)^3 dx → u-bounds 1 to 2 → ∫₁² u^3 du = 15/4

COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID (from Unit 3 post-quiz analysis — 33% miss rate on this KC):
✗ Forgetting to divide by the constant from du (e.g., ∫ sin(3x) dx missing the 1/3)
✗ Leaving x's in the integrand after substituting
✗ Forgetting to update bounds on definite integrals
✗ Picking u as the outer function instead of the inner
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Unit 3 post-quiz showed 2/6 students missed integration_by_substitution and stu_di scored 0. Spend extra class time on the "divide by the constant from du" error (sin(3x) example) and on changing bounds for definite integrals. Link to the new Extra Practice quiz for self-paced reinforcement.

arguments.message:
Hi everyone,

Now that Unit 3 is complete, I've analyzed your learning gains from the midterm to the Week 12 practice quiz and want to share both the good news and the area we're going to reinforce.

**What went well 🎉**
Class-wide gains on the chain rule for implicit functions were strong — mastery jumped from 17% (1/6 correct) on the midterm to 67% (4/6 correct) on the Week 12 quiz. Several of you posted +2 or +3 point gains. Excellent work.

**Where we're going to push harder**
The weakest knowledge component on the post-quiz was **integration by substitution (u-substitution)** — about 1 in 3 of you missed it. Because u-sub is foundational for Unit 4 and a guaranteed topic on the final, I'm rolling out two resources today:

1. **Updated Week 12 integration lecture slide** — the u-substitution slide now includes a 6-step recipe, three fully worked examples (polynomial, exponential, and trigonometric composites — including the tricky ∫sin(3x)dx case), and a list of the most common errors from your post-quiz responses.

2. **New "Extra Practice — Integration by Substitution" quiz** in Canvas — six questions, 20-minute limit, ungraded practice. Strongly recommended for anyone who got less than full marks on the Week 12 quiz, and a great warm-up for everyone before Unit 4.

Please complete the practice quiz by the end of this week so we can hit the ground running.

Office hours are open as usual — bring your u-sub questions!

— Your CALC101 instructor

instructions.task_instructions:
Evaluate the PHYS101_F24 tutoring intervention. The trap is that within-group improvement alone is not evidence of effectiveness, because natural improvement and regression-to-the-mean can produce midterm-to-final gains even without a real intervention effect. A clean effectiveness estimate needs a control group, so first check whether one actually exists in the data before framing any difference-in-gains claim.

Compute named per-student pre/post scores for at least three students and the whole-class average midterm-to-final gain. Use the F23 baseline mean you computed and the typical natural improvement range (about 5-15pp) as context for interpreting whether the gain is meaningful.

Send `advisor_phys101` a detailed private effectiveness report with the per-student scores, the whole-class gain, F23-anchored interpretation (citing the baseline mean and cohort size you computed), verdict, and a concrete next-step recommendation. Because there is no clean control arm and the sample is tiny, say so and recommend narrowing/refining the intervention (toward the KC that stays at 0% mastery on the final) and running a properly controlled larger cohort rather than blindly scaling. arguments.description: Practice quiz targeting the three knowledge components that showed the weakest class-wide mastery on the F23 midterm: product_rule_proof, piecewise_differentiability, and functional_equations. choices.A: It allows the numerator to be factored as a single product, eliminating the need for limits.
choices.B: It splits the difference quotient into two pieces, each of which becomes a derivative of f or g multiplied by a continuous factor as h → 0.
choices.C: It cancels the h in the denominator algebraically without using any limit.
choices.D: It converts the product rule into the quotient rule.

questions.question_text: [KC: product_rule_proof] Using the limit definition of the derivative, the product rule states that (fg)'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x). Which algebraic step in the proof of the product rule is justified by ADDING AND SUBTRACTING the term f(x+h)g(x) in the numerator of the difference quotient [f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x)]/h ?

choices.A: Only continuity at x = 1, i.e., a + b = 1.
choices.B: Only matching slopes at x = 1, i.e., a = 2.
choices.C: Both continuity (a + b = 1) and matching one-sided derivatives (a = 2), giving a = 2, b = -1.
choices.D: It is impossible for any choice of a and b.

questions.question_text: [KC: piecewise_differentiability] Let f(x) = x^2 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = ax + b for x > 1. For f to be DIFFERENTIABLE at x = 1, which conditions must hold?

choices.D: f'(x) depends on x and cannot be determined.

questions.question_text: [KC: functional_equations] Suppose f is a differentiable function satisfying f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) for all real x, y, and f'(0) = 3. What is f'(x) for all x?

choices.A: g is differentiable at x = 0 with g'(0) = 0.
choices.B: g is continuous at x = 0 but NOT differentiable there, because the one-sided derivatives are -1 and +1.
choices.C: g is neither continuous nor differentiable at x = 0.
choices.D: g is differentiable at x = 0 with g'(0) = 1.

questions.question_text: [KC: piecewise_differentiability] Which statement about the function g(x) = |x| at x = 0 is correct?

arguments.body:
Hi,

Proposing the following TA-hour split for the coming week, based on a comparison of F24 at-risk indicators against the F23 midterm baseline pulled from Canvas:

PROPOSED ALLOCATION (3 hours total)
- CALC101_F24: 2 hours
- STAT201_F24: 1 hour

JUSTIFICATION

1) F24 at-risk counts vs. F23 (at-risk = current grade < 60%):
   - CALC101_F24: ~76 students below 60% in the current gradebook, vs. F23 baseline of 32/120. This is a sharp upward shift — at-risk prevalence is roughly 2.4× the F23 cohort.
   - STAT201_F24: 4 of 6 enrolled students currently below 60%, vs. F23 baseline of 24/120 (20%). Proportionally elevated, but on a far smaller absolute base.

2) F23 historical KC weakness profile (using actual Canvas KC tags):
   - CALC101_F23 bottom-tier KCs: product_rule_proof, piecewise_differentiability, functional_equations — these showed the lowest class-wide mastery on the F23 midterm (correct rates near or below the bottom quartile across all 15 KCs assessed).
   - STAT201_F23 bottom-tier KCs: law_of_total_probability, summing_over_event_set, bayes_theorem — weak but less severe than CALC101's bottom three.

3) Conclusion: CALC101_F24 satisfies BOTH criteria for the larger share — more at-risk students in absolute terms AND a deeper historical KC weakness profile that is reappearing this term in current weak-KC tags (chain_rule_for_implicit_functions, piecewise_differentiability, product_rule_proof remain dominant weak KCs for current at-risk students).

ACTIONS ALREADY TAKEN
- Posted a targeted practice quiz in CALC101_F24 covering the three F23 bottom-tier KCs (product_rule_proof, piecewise_differentiability, functional_equations) with 4 questions across recall, conceptual, and application levels.
- Will post course-wide announcements in both CALC101_F24 and STAT201_F24 explaining the F23-anchored rationale.

A couple of caveats worth flagging:
- The "38 / 22" at-risk counts originally cited do not match what I see in Canvas. CALC101 is roughly double the cited figure; STAT201 has only 6 enrolled students in the system, so the "22" cannot be reproduced. I used the verified Canvas numbers above for the decision.
- Note: per the instructor's request, no individual outreach was sent to stu_dl (Jordan Park), who is a top performer in both courses and not relevant to this intervention.

Happy to revisit the split if you have additional context I'm missing.

Thanks.

arguments.new_body:
Key idea: A matrix A acts on vectors as a linear transformation (rotation, scaling, shearing).

• Most vectors get rotated AND scaled by A
• Eigenvectors are SPECIAL: they are only SCALED, never rotated
• The scaling factor is the eigenvalue λ:   A·v = λ·v
• λ > 1: stretch  |  0 < λ < 1: shrink  |  λ < 0: flip direction

In the figure: the red arrows show the eigenvectors — notice they stay on the same line after the transformation, only their length changes. The blue arrows (non-eigenvectors) get rotated off their original direction.
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Spend extra time here — quiz data shows 0/6 students got the geometric meaning of eigenvalues correct. Demonstrate live: draw a 2D grid, apply the transformation, and highlight which arrows stay on their span.
arguments.new_title: Geometric Intuition: What Eigenvectors Really Are

arguments.new_body:
Diagonalisation = changing to the "eigenvector coordinate system" where A acts as pure scaling.

Geometric reading of A = PDP⁻¹:
• P⁻¹: rotate space so eigenvectors align with standard axes
• D:   scale along each axis by λᵢ (pure stretch/shrink)
• P:   rotate back to the original coordinate frame

In the figure: the red arrows are the eigenvectors of A. After applying A, they remain on the same line — only their length changes by the factor λ. The grid lines show how the rest of space is sheared/rotated around these invariant directions.

Procedure:
1. Find eigenvalues: solve det(A - λI) = 0
2. Find eigenvectors: solve (A - λI)x = 0
3. P = [v₁ | v₂ | ... | vₙ],  D = diag(λ₁, ..., λₙ)
arguments.new_speaker_notes: Emphasize the geometric story: diagonalisation is "find the coordinate system where A is just scaling." Tie back to the visual on slide 1.
arguments.new_title: Visualizing the Transformation A = PDP⁻¹

arguments.body:
Hi,

I've updated the Week 6 Diagonalisation presentation (prs_math201_w6_diagonalisation) to better support students who are struggling with the abstract nature of eigenvalues/eigenvectors. The midterm quiz data motivated this revision: 0 of 6 students answered the "geometric meaning of eigenvalue" question correctly, and the overall class average on that quiz was 0.5/4.

Summary of visual improvements:

1. Slide 1 — retitled "Geometric Intuition: What Eigenvectors Really Are"
   • Added a geometric visualization image (eigenvector_geometric_transformation.png) showing eigenvectors as red arrows that are scaled but not rotated by the transformation, contrasted with blue non-eigenvectors that get rotated off their original direction.
   • Rewrote the body text to emphasize the core idea A·v = λ·v as "scaling without rotation," with intuition for λ > 1, 0 < λ < 1, and λ < 0.
   • Added speaker notes flagging the quiz performance gap and recommending a live board demonstration.

2. Slide 2 — retitled "Visualizing the Transformation A = PDP⁻¹"
   • Replaced the previous image with matrix_transformation_eigen_visualization.png, which illustrates how P⁻¹, D, and P act geometrically (rotate → scale → rotate back).
   • Added narrative text explaining that diagonalisation amounts to finding the coordinate system where A acts as pure scaling along the eigenvector directions.
   • Preserved the original procedural steps so the computational workflow remains intact.

Both image links contain the keywords "eigen", "transformation", and "geometric" as required. The goal is to give students a concrete mental picture they can fall back on when the algebra feels abstract.

Happy to discuss further or iterate based on classroom feedback.

Best,
Teaching Agent

questions.question_text: A PV diagram shows two gases A and B in the same rigid container. The total pressure curve is above each component curve. Which reading should be used for Dalton's Law before applying PV=nRT to gas A?

choices.A: Use total pressure directly as gas A's pressure.
choices.B: Use gas A's partial-pressure curve, then combine partial pressures only when finding total pressure.
choices.C: Ignore pressure because volume is fixed.
choices.D: Use the vapor-pressure value for gas A.

questions.question_text: A graph shows a gas moving from state 1 to state 2 with both pressure and temperature changing. Which interpretation explains why simply reading one PV=nRT snapshot is not enough?

choices.A: Both states must be related with P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2.
choices.C: Temperature can stay in Celsius because the graph has axes.
choices.D: Moles always double when volume doubles.

structure.title: Kinematics Review — Data-Driven Focus

bullets: Core equation:  x(t) = x₀ + v₀ t + ½ a t²
'Quadratic in t' means displacement curves over time when a ≠ 0
Common error: treating x(t) as linear (forgetting ½ a t² term)
When solving for t given x: rearrange to a t² + b t + c = 0 → quadratic formula
Sign convention: choose +x direction first, then assign signs to v₀ and a
structure.notes: Walk through the equation term-by-term. Emphasize that the ½at² term is the source of every 'why doesn't my answer match' moment.
structure.title: Constant Acceleration & the Quadratic Displacement–Time Relation

bullets: Average velocity:  v_avg = Δx / Δt   (slope of secant on x–t graph)
Instantaneous velocity:  v(t) = dx/dt   (slope of tangent on x–t graph)
For constant acceleration:  v_avg = (v₀ + v_f) / 2
Common error: using v_avg in place of v(t) for non-uniform motion
Diagnostic question: 'If a car speeds up, is v at midpoint = v_avg?' (No)
structure.notes: Use a v–t graph sketch. Pause and ask students which slope corresponds to which quantity.
structure.title: Average vs. Instantaneous Velocity

bullets: Decompose: horizontal (a_x=0, v_x=v₀cosθ) and vertical (a_y=-g, v_y0=v₀sinθ)
Time-of-flight on level ground:  T = 2 v₀ sinθ / g
Range:  R = v₀² sin(2θ) / g
Common errors: mixing x- and y-equations; forgetting that g acts only vertically
Procedure: (1) decompose, (2) write y(t)=0 to find T, (3) substitute T into x(t) for R
structure.notes: Stress the procedural sequence. The #1 reason for the 21% pass rate on time-of-flight was students attempting to solve x and y simultaneously instead of decomposing.
structure.title: Projectile Motion & Time-of-Flight

arguments.description: Practice quiz targeting the weakest kinematics KCs from the F23 midterm: projectile time-of-flight, quadratic displacement-time relation, projectile motion, and average vs. instantaneous velocity. Covers Remember, Understand, Apply, and Analyze Bloom levels.

questions.question_text: [Remember] In the equation x(t) = x₀ + v₀ t + ½ a t², which term makes the relationship quadratic in time?

choices.A: The slope of the secant line between t=0 and t
choices.B: The slope of the tangent line at time t
choices.C: The area under the curve up to time t
choices.D: The value of x(t) divided by t

questions.question_text: [Understand] On a position–time graph, instantaneous velocity at time t corresponds to:
[Apply] A ball is thrown straight up with v₀ = 20 m/s from ground level (g = 10 m/s²). Using y(t) = v₀ t − ½ g t², what is the total time of flight before it returns to the ground?
[Apply] A projectile is launched at 30 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal (g = 10 m/s²). What is its horizontal range on level ground? (R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g)
[Apply] A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over a 200 m distance. What is its acceleration? (Use v_f² = v₀² + 2aΔx)
[Analyze] A student claims: 'For any motion, the average velocity over an interval equals the instantaneous velocity at the midpoint of the time interval.' This claim is:

choices.A: Ball A, because it has more energy
choices.B: Ball B, because it falls straight down
choices.C: They hit at the same time — horizontal velocity does not affect vertical fall time

questions.question_text: [Analyze] Two balls are launched from the same height: Ball A horizontally at 10 m/s, Ball B at rest (dropped). Which hits the ground first?

arguments.title: Kinematics Review Practice Quiz (F23-data-informed)

new_bullets: The four constant-acceleration kinematic equations:
(1)  v = v₀ + a t
(2)  x = x₀ + v₀ t + ½ a t²   (quadratic in t)
(3)  v² = v₀² + 2 a (x − x₀)   (no t)
(4)  x = x₀ + ½ (v₀ + v) t           (no a)
Variables: position x, velocity v, acceleration a (constant), time t
Selecting the right equation: identify the unknown and the variable NOT given
Sign convention: pick +x direction first; assign signs to v₀ and a accordingly
F23 midterm context: only ~33% mastered constant-acceleration equations; ~26% the quadratic x–t relation
arguments.new_notes: Frame this as the toolkit students need before doing problems. Emphasize that equation (2) is quadratic in t — the source of most F23 errors on the displacement-time KC.
arguments.new_title: Kinematic Equations Overview

new_bullets: Targets weakest F23 KCs: quadratic displacement–time (~26%) and constant-acceleration equations (~33%)
Standard solution procedure:
1. List knowns/unknowns and choose +x direction
2. Pick the kinematic equation missing the irrelevant variable
3. Substitute, solve algebraically, then plug in numbers
4. Check units and sign of the answer
Common pitfalls: dropping the ½ a t² term; sign error on a; using v_avg when v(t) is needed
Worked examples to be added next (3 numerical problems)

arguments.new_title: Constant Acceleration Problems

new_bullets: F23 KC pass rates: projectile_motion ~28%, projectile_time_of_flight ~21% (the weakest of all)
Key idea: decompose into independent horizontal & vertical 1-D motions
Horizontal:  a_x = 0,    v_x = v₀ cosθ         x(t) = v₀ cosθ · t
Vertical:    a_y = −g,  v_y0 = v₀ sinθ       y(t) = v₀ sinθ · t − ½ g t²
Time-of-flight (level ground):  T = 2 v₀ sinθ / g
Range (level ground):           R = v₀² sin(2θ) / g
Maximum height:                 H = (v₀ sinθ)² / (2g)
Common error: trying to solve x and y simultaneously instead of decomposing
Procedure: (1) decompose, (2) set y(t)=0 → solve quadratic for T, (3) sub into x(t) for R
arguments.new_notes: Reinforce that horizontal and vertical motions are independent and share only t. The 21% pass rate on time-of-flight came from students who never decomposed.
arguments.new_title: Projectile Motion

new_bullets: P1. A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over 200 m. Find a.
Answer: a = 2 m/s²  (use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx)
P2. Ball thrown straight up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Find total time of flight.
Answer: T = 4 s   (set y(t)=0: 20t − 5t² = 0 → t = 0 or t = 4)
P3. Object dropped from rest falls for 3 s (g = 10 m/s²). Find distance fallen.
Answer: Δy = 45 m  (Δy = ½ g t² = ½ · 10 · 9)
P4. Projectile launched at 30 m/s, 30° above horizontal (g = 10 m/s²). Find range.
Answer: R = 78 m  (R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g = 900 · sin60° /10 ≈ 77.9)
P5. Car at 25 m/s brakes at −5 m/s². How far before stopping?
Answer: Δx = 62.5 m  (0 = 25² + 2(−5)Δx)
Self-check: redo each without looking; if stuck, revisit slide 0 or 1
arguments.new_notes: Have students attempt each problem independently first, then walk through. P2 and P4 specifically target the weakest F23 KCs (time-of-flight, projectile motion).
arguments.new_title: Practice Problems with Answers

new_bullets: Targets weakest F23 KCs: quadratic displacement–time (~26%), kinematic equations (~33%)
EXAMPLE 1 — Stopping distance (no time given → use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx)
Given: v₀ = 20 m/s, v = 0, a = −4 m/s².  Find Δx.
Step 1: 0² = 20² + 2(−4)Δx
EXAMPLE 2 — Find time from displacement (quadratic in t)
Given: x₀ = 0, v₀ = 5 m/s, a = 2 m/s², x = 24 m.  Find t.
Step 3: t = 3 s  (reject t = −8 s); check v = v₀ + a t = 5 + 2(3) = 11 m/s
EXAMPLE 3 — Two-stage motion (accelerate, then cruise)
Stage A: starts at rest, a = 2 m/s² for 5 s.  Stage B: constant velocity for 10 s.
Stage A: v = v₀ + a t = 0 + 2(5) = 10 m/s; Δx_A = ½ a t² = ½(2)(5²) = 25 m
Stage B: Δx_B = v · t = 10(10) = 100 m
Total: Δx = 25 + 100 = 125 m   (total time = 15 s)
arguments.new_notes: Walk through each example slowly. Example 1 shows when to skip the time variable. Example 2 directly addresses the F23 weakness on quadratic displacement-time: students must recognize the quadratic and apply the quadratic formula. Example 3 reinforces that you choose the right equation per stage and that v at end of Stage A is v0 of Stage B.

bullets: quiz_chem10_mid shows 0/6 on daltons_law_of_partial_pressures, vapor_pressure_correction, and stoichiometry_mole_calculations
Focus this review on gas collection over water and pressure corrections

structure.title: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
bullets: Total pressure is the sum of gas partial pressures
For gas collected over water: P_total = P_gas + P_water_vapor
Common pitfall: adding water vapor pressure to isolate dry gas pressure
structure.notes: Target KC: daltons_law_of_partial_pressures.

structure.title: Vapor Pressure Correction
bullets: Mnemonic: DRY gas pressure = TOTAL pressure - WATER vapor pressure
Worked example: P_total 755.0 mmHg, P_water 23.8 mmHg, so P_O2 = 731.2 mmHg
Pitfall: using 778.8 mmHg by adding instead of subtracting
structure.notes: Target KC: vapor_pressure_correction.

structure.title: Stoichiometry Link
bullets: Convert corrected gas pressure to moles with PV = nRT
Use mole ratio to connect O2 to reactant mass
Check units before percent purity
structure.notes: Target KC: stoichiometry_mole_calculations.

Annotate which pressure enters PV = nRT
Use the quiz to diagnose whether the misconception is pressure correction or mole conversion

arguments.title: CS101 Asymptotic Growth Remediation Quiz

questions.question_text: Target KC: asymptotic_dominance_polynomial_vs_loglinear. Which grows faster for large n: n^2 or n log n? Explain using the ratio n^2/(n log n).

answers.text: n^2 grows faster because n^2/(n log n)=n/log n tends to infinity.
n log n grows faster because it contains a logarithm.

questions.question_text: Target KC: logarithm_properties_and_growth. Simplify log(n^3) and use it to compare n log(n^3) with n log n.

answers.text: log(n^3)=3log n, so n log(n^3)=3n log n and has the same asymptotic class as n log n.
log(n^3)=log n^3 makes the function cubic.

questions.question_text: Target KC: growth_rate_comparison_for_large_n. Order log n, n, n log n, and n^2 from slowest to fastest growth and justify one adjacent comparison.

answers.text: log n < n < n log n < n^2; for example, n^2/(n log n)=n/log n grows without bound.
n^2 < n log n < n < log n.

questions.question_text: A model has 99% training accuracy and 62% validation accuracy. Which pattern best diagnoses overfitting_definition_and_diagnosis?

answers.text: High variance / overfitting: training performance is much better than validation performance.
High bias only: both train and validation performance are equally low.

questions.question_text: bias_variance_tradeoff_formal: Increasing model complexity usually decreases bias but can increase what quantity that causes sensitivity to the training sample?

answers.text: The number of labels in the dataset

questions.question_text: regularization_as_variance_reduction: What is the usual effect of increasing L2 regularization from an under-regularized model?

answers.text: It shrinks weights, often increasing bias but reducing variance.
It reduces both bias and variance to zero.

questions.question_text: Srivastava et al. dropout question: why can randomly omitting hidden units during training reduce overfitting?

answers.text: It discourages co-adaptation and acts like a regularizer/ensemble approximation.
It guarantees the training loss is always zero.

arguments.query: law of total probability misconception partition sample space students

bullets: Root misconception identified from F24 + F23 quiz data
Students treat P(B) as a single conditional probability instead of a weighted sum over a partition
F24 midterm: 4/6 missed summing-over-event-set, 5/6 missed Law of Total Probability
F23 midterm (n=120): same paired-failure pattern confirmed
Goal: build the 'partition the sample space, then weight' mental model
structure.notes: Frame the session: this is one misconception, not two. Both KCs collapse to the same operation: P(B) = Σ P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ).
structure.title: STAT201 Remediation: The Partition Mindset

bullets: Misconception: P(B) ≈ P(B|A) for the 'main' branch — students pick one conditional and stop
Secondary error: forgetting that {A₁,…,Aₖ} must be mutually exclusive AND exhaustive (probabilities sum to 1)
Evidence from F24 Q2: P(B|A₁)=0.8, P(B|A₂)=0.3, P(A₁)=0.4 — correct answer 0.50 = (0.8)(0.4)+(0.3)(0.6); common wrong answer 0.55 averages without weights
Research basis: Díaz & Batanero (2009) — 'transposed conditional' and base-rate neglect are dominant biases in intro-stat students
Batanero & Chernoff (2018) recommend explicit partition diagrams + worked examples before symbolic LTP
structure.notes: Cite the two papers so students see this is a documented, common difficulty — reduces shame, increases buy-in.
structure.title: Diagnosing the Root Cause

bullets: Scenario: 40% of emails are from known senders (A₁), 60% from unknown (A₂). P(spam | known)=0.05, P(spam | unknown)=0.55
STEP 1 — Identify partition: {A₁, A₂}. Check: disjoint ✓ and P(A₁)+P(A₂)=1 ✓
STEP 2 — Draw the tree: branch on Aᵢ first, then on B|Aᵢ
STEP 4 — Sum the matching leaves: P(B) = 0.02 + 0.33 = 0.35
Key insight: the answer is NEVER just P(B|A₁) — you must weight by how often each branch occurs
structure.notes: Walk through slowly on the board. Have students predict the answer BEFORE step 4 to surface the misconception.
structure.title: Worked Example — Partition a Sample Space

bullets: ACTIVITY (10 min, pairs): each pair gets 6 scenario cards (medical test, weather, manufacturing, etc.)
Task 1: For each card, identify the partition {Aᵢ} and verify Σ P(Aᵢ) = 1
Task 2: Sketch the probability tree; label each branch with P(Aᵢ) and P(B|Aᵢ)
Task 3: Compute P(B) using LTP and check with a peer
Debrief question: 'Which card tempted you to just report P(B|A₁)? Why?'
Goal: make the partition step visible and automatic — not skipped
structure.notes: The 'tempting card' debrief surfaces the exact misconception in students' own words.
structure.title: Interactive Activity — Partition Card Sort

bullets: P1. Factories A,B,C produce 50%, 30%, 20% of widgets; defect rates 1%, 2%, 3%. Find P(defective). [Answer: 0.017]
P2. 70% of students study; P(pass | study)=0.9, P(pass | not)=0.4. Find P(pass). [Answer: 0.75]
P3. (Trap) Given only P(B|A₁)=0.6 and P(A₁)=0.3, can you find P(B)? Explain what's missing. [Answer: No — need P(B|A₂) and partition must be exhaustive]
P4. Three urns chosen with probs 0.2, 0.5, 0.3; P(red ball) per urn is 0.4, 0.6, 0.1. Find P(red). [Answer: 0.41]
Self-check rubric: (a) Did I name the partition? (b) Do Aᵢ probs sum to 1? (c) Did I weight every branch?
structure.notes: Problem 3 is critical — it forces students to articulate WHY partial information isn't enough, exposing the misconception.
structure.title: Practice Problems (Target the Root Cause)

bullets: One rule to remember: P(B) = Σᵢ P(B|Aᵢ) · P(Aᵢ) — every term has TWO factors
Whenever you see a conditional probability problem, ask first: 'What's the partition?'
Connect forward: this same structure underlies Bayes' theorem — the denominator IS the LTP
Follow-up: complete the practice quiz on Canvas; office hours Thu for one-on-one walkthroughs
References: Díaz & Batanero (2009); Batanero & Chernoff (2018), Research on the Teaching and Learning of Probability
structure.notes: Emphasize the bridge to Bayes so students see the payoff. Reassure that this is a known sticking point, not a personal failure.
structure.title: Synthesis & Next Steps

arguments.body:
Hi,

I'm reaching out after reviewing your recent STAT201 midterm quiz results. Your score was 0/4, with all four probability knowledge components marked incorrect: conditional probability definition, summing over an event set, the Law of Total Probability, and discrete probability distributions.

The good news: looking at the class as a whole, the two questions most students struggled with (summing over an event set and the Law of Total Probability) actually share a single root cause — not recognizing that P(B) must be computed as a *weighted sum* over a partition of the sample space: P(B) = Σ P(B|Aᵢ)·P(Aᵢ). Once that one idea clicks, both topics tend to fall into place.

I've just posted a new remediation deck in Canvas called "stat201_prob_remediation.pptx" that targets exactly this misconception. It includes:
  • A worked partition example (spam-filter scenario)
  • An interactive partition card-sort activity
  • Four practice problems with a self-check rubric
  • References to research on common probability misconceptions, so you know this is a well-known sticking point

Please work through the deck before our next class, and come to office hours this week — I'd like to walk through problem 3 (the "trap" question) with you in person. You can absolutely recover from this; the misconception is fixable with focused practice.

Best,
Your STAT201 instructor

arguments.body:
Hi,

Flagging an at-risk student in STAT201_F24 and summarizing the class-level remediation I've put in place.

AT-RISK STUDENT
  • Student ID: stu_di
  • Midterm quiz score: 0/4 (0%) on quiz_stat20_mid
  • Per-KC: ALL four KCs incorrect — conditional_probability_definition, summing_over_event_set, law_of_total_probability, discrete_probability_distribution
  • This is the lowest score in the F24 cohort (n=6) and the only student missing every probability KC on the midterm.
  • I've sent a personalized Canvas message pointing them to the new remediation deck and inviting them to office hours.

DIAGNOSIS (data-grounded)
  • F24 midterm: 4/6 missed "summing over an event set" (Q2), 5/6 missed "Law of Total Probability" (Q3) — failures are paired.
  • F23 midterm validation (n=120): the same paired-failure pattern is present across the prior cohort, confirming this is a systemic conceptual issue, not a one-off.
  • Root cause: students do not treat P(B) as a weighted sum over a partition; they pick one conditional branch (e.g., P(B|A₁)) and stop, or average without weighting by P(Aᵢ).
  • Literature support: Díaz & Batanero (2009) on conditional-probability biases; Batanero & Chernoff (2018), Research on the Teaching and Learning of Probability.

REMEDIATION STEPS TAKEN
  1. Created a 6-slide remediation deck (stat201_prob_remediation.pptx) targeting the partition-and-weight mental model: worked example, interactive card-sort activity, 4 practice problems with self-check rubric, and synthesis bridging to Bayes' theorem.
  2. Sent a personalized Canvas message to stu_di citing their specific KC gaps and pointing to the new resources + office hours.

Please let me know if you'd like to coordinate additional outreach for stu_di (e.g., tutoring referral or check-in meeting).

Thanks,
STAT201 instructor

instructions.reason_for_call: I need a CALC101 item-analysis export and revision materials based on actual quiz evidence.
instructions.task_instructions:
For CALC101_F24, perform a data-grounded item/KC analysis using available quiz data.

Steps:
1. Inspect the CALC101 quiz list.
2. Retrieve submissions for the past-year midterm `quiz_calc101_f23_midterm` and the current midterm `quiz_calc10_mid`.
3. Compute item/KC difficulty as correct_count / total_attempts, expressed as a percentage rounded to one decimal place (e.g., 27/120 = 22.5%). The reported correct rate for every KC/item MUST equal this computed value exactly — do NOT round to whole numbers or estimate. Flag `PRIORITY_WEAK` when the correct rate is below 40%, `WATCH` when it is 40–50%, and `OK` otherwise.
4. Create a spreadsheet named EXACTLY `calc101_quiz_item_analysis.xlsx` (Excel file, via create_spreadsheet) with concrete rows for the analyzed KCs/items, including quiz ID, KC/item, correct/total, difficulty/correct rate (as the exact computed percentage), status flag, and recommended revision action. For the correct-rate column you may store the value either as a percentage string (e.g., `22.5%`) or as the equivalent numeric value (e.g., the number `22.5`, or the fraction `0.225` under an Excel percent format) — the literal `%` glyph is not required in the cell as long as the numeric value is the exact one-decimal rate.
5. Create a slide deck named EXACTLY `calc101_weak_item_revision.pptx` (PowerPoint slides, via create_slides — not a document or page) summarizing the top weak items and how the analysis should guide review priorities.
6. Post a CALC101_F24 announcement summarizing the highest-priority review targets.

Important: if a discrimination index is not available from the retrieved data, record it as not available rather than inventing one.
